You can use words or short labels you define.</p>\\r\\n    <label htmlFor={draftQuestion}>{embedded ? \'Your diagram\' : `Your diagram for sentence ${number}`}</label>\\r\\n    <textarea ref={draftInput} id={draftQuestion} className=\\"co-attempt-input\\" rows={3} value={draftDiagram} readOnly={comparing} onChange={event => setDraftDiagram(event.target.value)}/>\\r\\n    <label htmlFor={readbackQuestion}>{embedded ? \'Read it in English\' : `Your English readback for sentence ${number}`}</label>\\r\\n    <textarea id={readbackQuestion} className=\\"co-attempt-input\\" rows={3} value={draftReadback} readOnly={comparing} onChange={event => setDraftReadback(event.target.value)}/>\\r\\n    {!comparing && <button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"co-primary\\" disabled={!draftDiagram.trim() || !draftReadback.trim()} onClick={() => setComparing(true)}>{embedded ? \'Compare with the choices\' : `Compare my translation for sentence ${number}`}</button>}\\r\\n    {comparing && <>\\r\\n    <p>{embedded ? \\"Compare your written diagram with these choices. Check that you kept the complete conditions and the arrow\'s direction.\\" : \'Your written answer is saved for you to compare. The choices below check the target and direction; your written answer is not graded automatically.\'}</p>\\r\\n    <h3 id={targetQuestion}>In this sentence, what does <strong>{item.word}</strong> {item.family === \'sufficient\' ? \'make enough\' : \'make required\'}?</h3>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-choices\\" role=\\"group\\" aria-labelledby={targetQuestion}>{targetOptions(item, index).map(option => <button type=\\"button\\" key={option} aria-pressed={target === option} onClick={() => change(() => setTarget(option))}>{option}</button>)}</div>\\r\\n    <h3 id={sideQuestion}>Which condition gives you enough to establish the other?</h3>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-choices\\" role=\\"group\\" aria-labelledby={sideQuestion}>{sideOptions(item, index).map(option => <button type=\\"button\\" key={option} aria-pressed={left === option} onClick={() => change(() => setLeft(option))}>{option}</button>)}</div>\\r\\n    {left && <RuleDiagram left={left} right={left === item.left ? item.right : item.left} label={`Your diagram: ${left} implies ${left === item.left ? item.right : item.left}`}/>}\\r\\n    <div className=\\"cr-control-row\\"><button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"co-primary\\" disabled={target === null || left === null} onClick={() => { setChecked(true); onChecked(true); onResult?.({ targetCorrect, targetIncomplete: target === item.partial, sideCorrect }); }}>{embedded ? \'Check answer\' : `Check sentence ${number}`}</button><button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"cr-reset\\" onClick={reset}>{embedded ? \'Revise my answer\' : `Try sentence ${number} again`}</button></div>\\r\\n    <div role=\\"status\\">{checked && <div className={`co-feedback ${targetCorrect && sideCorrect ? \'co-correct\' : \'\'}`}>\\r\\n      {targetCorrect && sideCorrect ? <>\\r\\n        <strong>Read it back: {item.readback}</strong>\\r\\n        <p>{item.why}</p>\\r\\n      </> : <>\\r\\n      <strong>Revise the part described below.</strong>\\r\\n      <p>{targetCorrect ? `You found the complete target: ${item.target}.` : target === item.partial ? item.partialFeedback : item.otherFeedback}</p>\\r\\n      <p>{sideCorrect ? \'Your arrow keeps the direction the sentence gives.\' : item.reversed}</p>\\r\\n      <p>Here, <strong>{item.word}</strong> points to what is {item.family === \'sufficient\' ? \'enough, so its target goes on the left\' : \'required, so its target goes on the right\'}. {item.why}</p>\\r\\n      <p>Read it back: {item.readback}</p>\\r\\n      </>}\\r\\n    </div>}</div>\\r\\n    </>}\\r\\n    {!comparing && <button type=\\"button\\" className=\\"cr-reset\\" onClick={reset}>{embedded ? \'Revise my answer\' : `Try sentence ${number} again`}</button>}\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function MixedFamilyPractice() {\\r\\n  const [current, setCurrent] = useState(0);\\r\\n  const [checked, setChecked] = useState<boolean[]>(() => mixedFamilyItems.map(() => false));\\r\\n  return <>\\r\\n    <p>These sentences use both kinds of expression. The family name stays hidden until you check your choices. First translate each sentence yourself, without supplied condition labels. Then compare your work and check the complete target and arrow direction before moving on.</p>\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-kicker\\" role=\\"status\\">Sentence {current + 1} of {mixedFamilyItems.length}</p>\\r\\n    {mixedFamilyItems.map((item, index) => <div key={item.sentence} hidden={current !== index}><MixedItemCheck item={item} index={index} onChecked={value => setChecked(previous => previous.map((old, itemIndex) => itemIndex === index ? value : old))}/></div>)}\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-choices\\"><button type=\\"button\\" disabled={current === 0} onClick={() => setCurrent(current - 1)}>Previous mixed sentence</button><button type=\\"button\\" disabled={current === mixedFamilyItems.length - 1 || !checked[current]} onClick={() => setCurrent(current + 1)}>Next mixed sentence</button></div>\\r\\n    <p>Moving between sentences keeps your written attempt, choices, and feedback. Trying a sentence again keeps your writing so you can revise it, and hides the supplied labels until you compare again.</p>\\r\\n  </>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n"}'}]

## Tool: exec

function lin(v){v/=255;return v<=.04045?v/12.92:((v+.055)/1.055)**2.4}
function lum(rgb){return rgb.map(lin).reduce((s,x,i)=>s+x*[.2126,.7152,.0722][i],0)}
function ratio(a,b){let l=[lum(a),lum(b)].sort((a,b)=>b-a);return(l[0]+.05)/(l[1]+.05)}
for(let a of [.46,.5]){let bg=[245,242,237],fg=bg.map((v,i)=>[26,26,a===.5?23:26][i]*a+v*(1-a));text({alpha:a,fg,bg,contrast:ratio(fg,bg)});}
function oklch(L,C,h){h*=Math.PI/180;let a=C*Math.cos(h),b=C*Math.sin(h);let l=(L+.3963377774*a+.2158037573*b)**3,m=(L-.1055613458*a-.0638541728*b)**3,s=(L-.0894841775*a-1.291485548*b)**3;let rgb=[4.0767416621*l-3.3077115913*m+.2309699292*s,-1.2684380046*l+2.6097574011*m-.3413193965*s,-.0041960863*l-.7034186147*m+1.707614701*s];return rgb.map(v=>255*(v<=.0031308?12.92*v:1.055*v**(1/2.4)-.055));}
text({main:ratio(oklch(.29,.035,175),oklch(.99,.008,90)),muted:ratio(oklch(.44,.03,170),[255,253,246]),cta:ratio(oklch(.99,.008,90),oklch(.43,.075,174)),border:ratio(oklch(.63,.03,164),oklch(.99,.008,90))});

In Brief\nL25: \nL26: Goal\nL27:     Text can be seen by more people.\nL28: What to do\nL29:     Provide sufficient contrast between text and its background.\nL30: Why it\'s important\nL31:     Some people cannot read faint text.\nL32: ## Success Criterion (SC)\nL33: \nL34: The visual presentation of \ue200cite\ue20215†text\ue201 and \ue200cite\ue20216†images of text\ue201 has a \ue200cite\ue20217†contrast ratio\ue201 of at least 4.5:1, except for the following:\nL35: \nL36: Large Text\nL37: \nL38: \nL39: \ue200cite\ue20218†Large-scale\ue201 text and images of large-scale text have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1;\nL40: \nL41: Incidental\nL42: Text or images of text that are part of an inactive \ue200cite\ue20219†user interface component\ue201 , that are \ue200cite\ue20220†pure decoration\ue201 , that are not visible to anyone, or that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content, have no contrast requirement.\nL43: \nL44: Logotypes\nL45: \nL46: \nL47: Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement.\nL48: ## Intent\nL49: \nL50: The intent of this success criterion is to provide enough contrast between text and its background, so that it can be read by people with moderately low vision or impaired contrast perception, without the use of contrast-enhancing assistive technology.\nL51: For all consumers of visual content, adequate light-dark contrast is needed between the relative luminance of text and its background for good readability. Many different visual impairments can substantially impact contrast sensitivity, requiring more light-dark contrast, regardless of color (hue). For people with color vision deficiency who are not able to distinguish certain shades of color, hue and saturation have minimal or no effect on legibility as assessed by reading performance.\nL52: Further, the inability to distinguish certain shades of color does not negatively affect light-dark contrast perception. Therefore, in the recommendation, contrast is calculated in such a way that color (hue) is not a key factor.\nL53: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.\nL54: Text that is larger and has wider character strokes is easier to read at lower contrast. The contrast requirement for larger text is therefore lower. This allows authors to use a wider range of color choices for large text, which is helpful for design of pages, particularly titles. 18 point text or 14 point bold text is judged to be large enough to require a lower contrast ratio.\nL55: (See The American Printing House for the Blind Guidelines for Large Printing and The Library of Congress Guidelines for Large Print under \ue200cite\ue2029†Resources\ue201 ). "18 point" and "bold" can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient. Since there are so many different fonts, the general measures are used and a note regarding thin or unusual fonts is included in the definition for \ue200cite\ue20218†large-scale\ue201 text.\nL56: Note\nL57: \nL58: When evaluating this Success Criterion, the font size in points should be obtained from the user agent or calculated on font metrics in the way that user agents do. Point sizes are based on the CSS `pt` size as defined in \ue200cite\ue20221†CSS3 Values\ue201 . The ratio between sizes in points and CSS pixels is `1pt = 1.333px`, therefore `14pt` and `18pt` are equivalent to approximately `18.5px` and `24px`.\nL59: Because different image editing applications default to different pixel densities (e.g., `72ppi` or `96ppi`), specifying point sizes for fonts from within an image editing application can be unreliable when it comes to presenting text at a specific size. When creating images of large-scale text, authors should ensure that the text in the resulting image is roughly equivalent to 1.2 and 1.5 em or to 120% or 150% of the default size for body text.\nL60: For example, for a `72ppi` image, an author would need to use approximately 19pt and 24pt font sizes in order to successfully present images of large-scale text to a user.\nL61: The 3:1 and 4.5:1 contrast ratios referenced in this success criterion are intended to be treated as threshold values. When comparing the computed contrast ratio to the Success Criterion ratio, the computed values should not be rounded (e.g., 4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold).\nL62: \nL63: Note\nL64: Because authors do not have control over user settings for font smoothing/anti-aliasing, when evaluating this Success Criterion, refer to the foreground and background colors obtained from the user agent, or the underlying markup and stylesheets, rather than the text as presented on screen.\nL65: Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin or unusual fonts may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter color than the actual text color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where text has a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but has a much lower contrast in practice.\nL66: In these cases, best practice would be for authors to choose a font with stronger/thicker lines, or to aim for a foreground/background color combination that exceeds the normative requirements of this success criterion.\nL67: The contrast requirements for text also apply to images of text (text that has been rendered into pixels and then stored in an image format) - see \ue200cite\ue20222†Success Criterion 1.4.5 Images of Text\ue201 .\nL68: \nL69: This requirement applies to situations in which images of text were intended to be understood as text. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included. Nor is text that for some reason is designed to be invisible or hard to discern to all viewers.\nL70: Beyond logos and logotypes, text that has insufficient contrast due to corporate identity or brand guidelines is not exempted from the requirements of this criterion.\nL71: \nL72: In this provision there is an exception that reads "that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,". This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.\nL73: \nL74: Note\nL75: Images of text do not scale as well as text because they tend to pixelate. It is also harder to change foreground and background contrast and color combinations for images of text, which is necessary for some users. Therefore, we suggest using text wherever possible, and when not, consider supplying an image of higher resolution.\nL76: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.\nL77: \nL78: Although this success criterion only applies to text, similar issues occur for content presented in charts, graphs, diagrams, and other non-text-based information, which is covered by \ue200cite\ue20223†Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non-Text Contrast\ue201 .\nL79: \nL80: Note\nL81: There are cases where text is heavily stylized – for instance, using a very ornate or distorted typeface – to the point where it acts more as a graphic, rather than text. Similarly, there are situations where text characters are used as symbols – used for their visual appearance, rather than "expressing something in human language". These cases fall under the definition of \ue200cite\ue20224†non-text content\ue201 and the requirements of \ue200cite\ue20223†1.4.11 Non-text Contrast\ue201 .\nL82: Figure 1. Text using a geometric typeface – arguably acting as an image/non-text content.\nL83: \nL84: Figure 2. Even though the two buttons use text characters — an uppercase "X", often used for "Close" buttons, and a ">" character, to act as a right-pointing arrow — they count as non-text characters/symbols. Their contrast ratio of just above 3:1 passes \ue200cite\ue20223†Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non-Text Contrast\ue201 .\nL85: \nL86: See also \ue200cite\ue20225†1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)\ue201 .\nL87: ### Logos\nL88: \nL89: Text used as part of a logo or logotype is exempted from contrast requirements, under the assumption that logos/logotypes must comply with stricter color choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines.\nL90: However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as \ue200cite\ue20219†user interface components\ue201 (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a recommended practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast, if allowed by the corporate identity or brand guidelines. Alternatively, authors should consider providing an equivalent \ue200cite\ue20219†user interface component\ue201 which serves the same purpose and meets contrast requirements.\nL91: If logos normally have sufficient contrast but are presented with an insufficient contrast as an author choice, rather than because of corporate identity or brand guidelines, then that particular low contrast presentation is not exempt from the contrast requirements.\nL92: \ue200cite\ue20226†Image: A heading: \'ACME tool is trusted by the world\'s most innovative companies.\'; below the heading, a series of nine company logos, all presented as very dark grey logos on the page\'s black background, with very low contrast; one logo is hovered with the mouse, and is displayed in white, with high contrast against the page background.\ue201 L93: Figure 3. An author chooses to present company logos with low contrast by default, until they are hovered; the fact that these are logos doesn\'t exempt this scenario from failing the requirements of this success criterion, as the initial low contrast presentation is not "essential".\nL94: ### Rationale for the Ratios Chosen\nL95: \nL96: A contrast ratio of 3:1 is the minimum level recommended by [\ue200cite\ue20227†ISO-9241-3\ue201 ] and [\ue200cite\ue20228†ANSI-HFES-100-1988\ue201 ] for standard text and vision. The 4.5:1 ratio is used in this success criterion to account for the loss in contrast that results from moderately low visual acuity, congenital or acquired color deficiencies, or the loss of contrast sensitivity that typically accompanies aging.\nL97: The rationale is based on a) adoption of the 3:1 contrast ratio for minimum acceptable contrast for normal observers, in the ANSI standard, and b) the empirical finding that in the population, visual acuity of 20/40 is associated with a contrast sensitivity loss of roughly 1.5 [\ue200cite\ue20229†ARDITI-FAYE\ue201 ]. A user with 20/40 would thus require a contrast ratio of `3 * 1.5 = 4.5 to 1`. Following analogous empirical findings and the same logic, the user with 20/80 visual acuity would require contrast of about 7:1.\nL98: This ratio is used in Success Criterion 1.4.6.\nL99: Hues are perceived differently by users with color vision deficiencies (both congenital and acquired) resulting in different colors and relative luminance contrasts than for normally sighted users. Because of this, effective contrast and readability are different for this population. However, color deficiencies are so diverse that prescribing effective general use color pairs (for contrast) based on quantitative data is not feasible.\nL100: Requiring good luminance contrast accommodates this by requiring contrast that is independent of color perception. Fortunately, most of the luminance contribution is from the mid and long wave receptors which largely overlap in their spectral responses.\nL101: The result is that effective luminance contrast can generally be computed without regard to specific color deficiency, except for the use of predominantly long wavelength colors against darker colors (generally appearing black) for those who have protanopia. (We provide an advisory technique on avoiding red on black for that reason). For more information see [\ue200cite\ue20230†ARDITI-KNOBLAUCH-1994\ue201 ] [\ue200cite\ue20231†ARDITI-KNOBLAUCH-1996\ue201 ] [\ue200cite\ue20232†ARDITI\ue201 ].\nL102: Note\nL103: \nL104: Some people with cognitive disabilities require color combinations or hues that have low contrast, and therefore we allow and encourage authors to provide mechanisms to adjust the foreground and background colors of the content. Some of the combinations that could be chosen may have contrast levels that will be lower than those specified here. This is not a violation of this Success Criterion, provided there is a mechanism that will return to the required values set out here.\nL105: The contrast ratio of 4.5:1 was chosen for level AA because it compensated for the loss in contrast sensitivity usually experienced by users with vision loss equivalent to approximately 20/40 vision. (20/40 calculates to approximately 4.5:1.) 20/40 is commonly reported as typical visual acuity of elders at roughly age 80. [\ue200cite\ue20233†GITTINGS-FOZARD\ue201 ]\nL106: The contrast ratio of 7:1 was chosen for level AAA because it compensated for the loss in contrast sensitivity usually experienced by users with vision loss equivalent to approximately 20/80 vision. People with more than this degree of vision loss usually use assistive technologies to access their content (and the assistive technologies usually have contrast enhancing, as well as magnification capability built into them).\nL107: The 7:1 level therefore generally provides compensation for the loss in contrast sensitivity experienced by users with low vision who do not use assistive technology and provides contrast enhancement for color deficiency as well.\nL108: Note\nL109: \nL110: Calculations in [\ue200cite\ue20227†ISO-9241-3\ue201 ] and [\ue200cite\ue20228†ANSI-HFES-100-1988\ue201 ] are for body text. A relaxed contrast ratio is provided for text that is much larger.\nL111: ### Notes on formula\nL112: \nL113: Conversion from nonlinear to linear RGB values is based on IEC/4WD 61966-2-1 [\ue200cite\ue20234†IEC-4WD\ue201 ].\nL114: \nL115: The formula (`L1/L2`) for contrast is based on [\ue200cite\ue20227†ISO-9241-3\ue201 ] and [\ue200cite\ue20228†ANSI-HFES-100-1988\ue201 ] standards.\nL116: \nL117: The ANSI/HFS 100-1988 standard calls for the contribution from ambient light to be included in the calculation of L1 and L2. The `.05` value used is based on Typical Viewing Flare from [\ue200cite\ue20234†IEC-4WD\ue201 ].\nL118: This success criterion and its definitions use the terms "contrast ratio" and "relative luminance" rather than "luminance" to reflect the fact that web content does not emit light itself. The contrast ratio gives a measure of the relative luminance that would result when displayed. (Because it is a ratio, it is dimensionless.)\nL119: \nL120: Note\nL121: \nL122: Refer to \ue200cite\ue2029†related resources\ue201 for a list of tools that utilize the contrast ratio to analyze the contrast of web content.\nL123: See also \ue200cite\ue20235†2.4.7 Focus Visible\ue201 for techniques for indicating keyboard focus.\nL124: ### Inactive User Interface Components\nL125: \nL126: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable. An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.\nL127: \nL128: Figure 4. An inactive button using default browser styles\nL129: ## Benefits\nL130: \n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nUnderstanding Success Criterion 2.5.5: Target Size (Enhanced) | WAI | W3C (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-enhanced.html)\n\ue200cite\ue202turn0view1\ue201 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; A page\'s location alone does not establish truth or sensitivity.\\r\\n\\r\\nLive systems remain authoritative for operational state: Calendar and Cal.com for scheduled or used sessions, LSAT U Supabase for homework, dossiers and publication state, Stripe for payments, and Gmail for correspondence. Mark local operational summaries with the date and system actually checked. On disagreement, the verified backend wins; preserve the discrepancy and its evidence. The brain is primary for local transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions that have no upstream owner.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use stable filenames and explicit evidence\\r\\n\\r\\nNew knowledge filenames use lowercase kebab-case and a descriptive title, for example `compiled-knowledge.md`. Use a date prefix only when the date identifies an event or source generation. Search the index and owning folder for the same subject before making a new page. Keep existing filenames, aliases, and scoped student conventions.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse relative Markdown links that resolve from the page, or existing Obsidian wikilinks with the actual filename. Display titles may differ from filenames. Link relevant related pages in the prose and maintain reciprocal links where the relationship helps navigation. Never invent a link target and leave it missing without labeling it as a gap.\\r\\n\\r\\nNew compiled knowledge pages use this minimal frontmatter, extending the existing `type`, `subject`, `updated`, and `aliases` convention:\\r\\n\\r\\n```yaml\\r\\n---\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\nsubject: Compiled knowledge\\r\\ncreated: 2026-09-30\\r\\nupdated: 2026-09-30\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\ntags: [llm-wiki]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nChoose an appropriate type such as `source`, `entity`, `concept`, `comparison`, or `synthesis`. `sources` contains relative links to supporting source summaries or evidence, not unverified attribution. Add a verification date and live-system name in the body when operational facts need freshness. Existing pages need not be retrofitted just to satisfy this template; preserve their metadata and domain conventions when editing.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis human-directed editing schema does not grant automated overwrite permissions. [The automation metadata schema](frontmatter.md) remains authoritative for `brain-managed`, `schema-version`, and `domain`. Do not add `brain-managed: true` to ordinary pages by default. Unattended automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections and uses compare-and-swap.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach source summary contains:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Source identity: title, author if known, original URL or supplied file, publication date if known, and capture date. Label unknowns rather than guessing.\\r\\n2. A relative archived-evidence link and SHA-256 or a link to its hash manifest.\\r\\n3. A factual account of what the source says, clearly attributed to it.\\r\\n4. Separate interpretation: why it matters here, what it supports or challenges, and limitations.\\r\\n5. Links to pages changed, unresolved questions, and any contradictions.\\r\\n\\r\\nArchive a clip under `raw/sources/clips/<slug>/` or a supplied document under `raw/sources/<slug>/` with its original contents, `PROVENANCE.md`, and `SHA256SUMS`. Record capture mechanism, original attachment/path or URL, dates, and transformations in provenance. Preserve original bytes; store any extracted text or conversion as a distinct derived artifact. Never follow a migration symlink outside its registered source root. A newer source generation is a new evidence artifact, not an overwrite of the old one.\\r\\n\\r\\nDistinguish source claims from verified facts and agent synthesis. Cite factual claims near the relevant passage with a link to a source summary, raw evidence, or verified live system. Do not present an article\'s assertion as established truth merely because it was ingested. Do not auto-promote transcripts or raw captures into native personal memory.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Ingest compiles one source into the existing knowledge\\r\\n\\r\\nNatural requests such as \\"ingest this\\", \\"add this to my second brain\\", and \\"process this article\\" enter one public workflow. Specialized session write-up requests use `post-session-recap`, which owns the finished student lesson and its intake; transcript filing does not silently create or send a lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Resolve the supplied source, owning domain, and scoped instructions. Check `wiki/index.md` and the appropriate domain index for an existing source or subject.\\r\\n2. Compute the source hash and compare available provenance or summaries for an identical source. Identical bytes do not need a second summary. A changed version keeps its own provenance and an explicit relationship to the earlier generation. Do not equate similar titles with identical contents.\\r\\n3. Copy evidence into the archive and verify hashes before compiling. Preserve originals. A processed inbox item may be recorded as processed without deletion; moving or deleting needs explicit authorization.\\r\\n4. Read the complete relevant source. For meaningful images, inspect them separately where supported; do not claim to have understood images from Markdown alt text alone.\\r\\n5. Present key takeaways and the pages they would affect. Default to one source at a time with Joshua involved. If he explicitly asks to implement the supplied source, this authorizes that source\'s integration without an extra approval loop; make routine filing choices and report them. Batch intake requires an explicit batch request.\\r\\n6. Write or update the source summary. Update relevant existing entities, concepts, domain records, comparisons, and synthesis. Preserve qualifications and explain changed conclusions. A source may touch 10–15 pages; that is a possibility, never a quota. Touch only pages whose content or useful connections actually change.\\r\\n7. Update the relevant indexes and reciprocal links. Record contradictory evidence with links to both claims and their dates. Leave the conflict explicitly unresolved until evidence or Joshua adjudicates it; do not silently replace one generation with another.\\r\\n8. Verify edited-page links, evidence paths and hashes, index entries, and the completeness of the intended changes. Append the ingest log entry and report what changed, what remains unresolved, and anything skipped.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first worked example is [the idea file\'s source summary](../../wiki/sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md), connected to [compiled knowledge](../../wiki/concepts/compiled-knowledge.md) and this operating schema. It illustrates source evidence, attributed summary, local synthesis, cross-links, index entries, and a dated ingest log without treating every claim in the idea file as proven.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Query starts with the index and compounds useful answers\\r\\n\\r\\nFor knowledge-bearing interactions, resolve the owning domain. Read `wiki/hot.md` when current-session context matters, then the appropriate index and linked pages. For a wiki query, the index comes before ad hoc searching raw files. Use `rg` to resolve omissions or scale limits, and escalate to a relevant source or live system when the compiled pages lack evidence or freshness.\\r\\n\\r\\nAnswer in plain language with links to the pages and evidence used. State uncertainty and unresolved conflicts. If the answer changes durable understanding, update its existing authoritative page. Create a new comparison or synthesis page only when it has a distinct lasting purpose; link it from the index and supporting pages. File useful findings, not every conversational sentence. Record filed query outputs in the log.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe schema applies to knowledge intake, questions, decisions, drafting, and maintenance. Mechanical shell/Git/file operations, self-contained code edits, and narrow skill inputs need not read the wiki merely to satisfy a ritual. A brief transient question does not require a new page or log entry. Do not use the schema to send messages, change a live backend, deploy, delete, or expose credentials outside existing authorization.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The index catalogs content; the log records changes\\r\\n\\r\\n`wiki/index.md` is the master content catalog. List every wiki page once in the complete catalog under a useful category (curated navigation links may also point to those pages) with a working link and one-line description. Include navigation links to `corpus/index.md`, `students/README.md`, this schema, and other authoritative external homes rather than flattening their full contents into the wiki index. Useful categories include hubs, entities, concepts, source summaries, comparisons/synthesis, operations, and references. Dates and source counts are optional; if present, keep them accurate. Update the index on every ingest and whenever pages or their purpose change. Run `py system/scripts/wiki-maintenance.py --index` to refresh its fenced generated catalog without replacing curated navigation; the script checks for concurrent edits before writing.\\r\\n\\r\\n`wiki/log.md` is append-only. Preserve old entries even when a conclusion changes; append a correction or superseding entry. New entries use:\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n## [2026-09-30] ingest | LLM Wiki pattern\\r\\n\\r\\n- Source: [source summary](sources/llm-wiki-pattern.md); provenance and SHA-256 linked there.\\r\\n- Changed: source summary, compiled-knowledge concept, operating schema, and index.\\r\\n- Finding: compile source knowledge into maintained linked pages; preserve current domain homes.\\r\\n- Verification: evidence hash, links, and index entries checked.\\r\\n- Open: any unresolved conflict or gap, or \\"None\\".\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse operation names `ingest`, `query`, `lint`, or `system`. Include source/output links, meaningful changed pages, findings, verification, and unresolved work as relevant. Absolute dates use Joshua\'s client timezone. A log is not a copied transcript, a credential store, or a substitute for `wiki/tasks.md`. Log locked decisions in `decisions/log.md` as well when the task actually locks a decision.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Lint keeps the compiled knowledge trustworthy\\r\\n\\r\\nRun a focused consistency check after each ingest or durable query edit. Run a broader lint when Joshua asks, after a substantial batch or structural change, or when retrieval exposes contradictions or broken navigation. Periodically suggest a wider check when the vault has accumulated unchecked changes; no scheduled automation is implied.\\r\\n\\r\\nRun `py system/scripts/wiki-maintenance.py --lint` for structural checks; results go to `system/generated/wiki-lint.generated.tsv`. This checks local links, source metadata, and possible orphans. It does not establish semantic truth, freshness, or completeness.\\r\\n\\r\\nInspect contradictory claims, facts superseded by newer evidence, stale operational snapshots, orphan pages without useful inbound links, missing targets, missing reciprocal links, concepts that merit a page, duplicate subject pages, absent provenance, and evidence gaps. Report each finding with affected links, why it matters, and a recommended correction or research question. Fix clear reversible link/index errors within authorized scope. Keep interpretive conflicts explicit and ask Joshua only where his judgment is required. Do not invent fresh evidence or silently merge incompatible claims. Append a lint entry with scope, fixes, unresolved findings, and verification limits.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Tools improve the workflow without becoming requirements\\r\\n\\r\\nMarkdown files, working links, the index, the log, and existing Git history are sufficient to start. Obsidian can browse pages and show the graph. Web Clipper can place new captures in the inbox. Locally stored attachments may make evidence more durable; inspect images explicitly and preserve provenance. Dataview, Marp, plots, canvases, or slide decks are optional output formats. A local search tool such as qmd is an option only if index navigation and ordinary text search cease to be adequate.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not install any tool or plugin merely to implement the pattern. Use existing connected capabilities and applicable skills. Protect exclusions before a Git commit or push; Markdown version history must not drag raw personal exports, credentials, or nested app repositories into the outer repository.\\r\\n"}}\n{"i":1,"status":"fulfilled","value":{"chunk_id":"63b907","wall_time_seconds":0.420537,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":20194,"output":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 20194)\\nTotal output lines: 310\\n\\n---\\r\\ntype: operating-layer\\r\\nsubject: Hot last-session cache\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-07\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Hot — last-session cache\\r\\n\\r\\nFreshest working state; the first page `/pickup` reads. and users\' mental state in context.\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify and improve unclear, confusing, or poorly written interface text to make the product easier to understand and use.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Assess Current Copy\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify what makes the text unclear or ineffective:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Find clarity problems**:\\r\\n   - **Jargon**: Technical terms users won\'t understand\\r\\n   - **Ambiguity**: Multiple interpretations possible\\r\\n   - **Passive voice**: \\"Your file has been uploaded\\" vs \\"We uploaded your file\\"\\r\\n   - **Length**: Too wordy or too terse\\r\\n   - **Assumptions**: Assuming user knowledge they don\'t have\\r\\n   - **Missing context**: Users don\'t know what to do or why\\r\\n   - **Tone mismatch**: Too formal, too casual, or inappropriate for situation\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Understand the context**:\\r\\n   - Who\'s the audience? (Technical? General? First-time users?)\\r\\n   - What\'s the user\'s mental state? (Stressed during error? Confident during success?)\\r\\n   - What\'s the action? (What do we want users to do?)\\r\\n   - What\'s the constraint? (Character limits? Space limitations?)\\r\\n\\r\\n**CRITICAL**: Clear copy helps users succeed. Unclear copy creates frustration, errors, and support tickets.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Plan Copy Improvements\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate a strategy for clearer communication:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Primary message**: What\'s the ONE thing users need to know?\\r\\n- **Action needed**: What should users do next (if anything)?\\r\\n- **Tone**: How should this feel? (Helpful? Apologetic? Encouraging?)\\r\\n- **Constraints**: Length limits, brand voice, localization considerations\\r\\n\\r\\n**IMPORTANT**: Good UX writing is invisible. Users should understand immediately without noticing the words.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Improve Copy Systematically\\r\\n\\r\\nRefine text across these common areas:\\r\\n\\r\\n### Error Messages\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Error 403: Forbidden\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"You don\'t have permission to view this page. Contact your admin for access.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Invalid input\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Email addresses need an @ symbol. Try: name@example.com\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Explain what went wrong in plain language\\r\\n- Suggest how to fix it\\r\\n- Don\'t blame the user\\r\\n- Include examples when helpful\\r\\n- Link to help/support if applicable\\r\\n\\r\\n### Form Labels & Instructions\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"DOB (MM/DD/YYYY)\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Date of birth\\" (with placeholder showing format)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Enter value here\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Your email address\\" or \\"Company name\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Use clear, specific labels (not generic placeholders)\\r\\n- Show format expectations with examples\\r\\n- Explain why you\'re asking (when not obvious)\\r\\n- Put instructions before the field, not after\\r\\n- Keep required field indicators clear\\r\\n\\r\\n### Button & CTA Text\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Click here\\" | \\"Submit\\" | \\"OK\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Create account\\" | \\"Save changes\\" | \\"Got it, thanks\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Describe the action specifically\\r\\n- Use active voice (verb + noun)\\r\\n- Match user\'s mental model\\r\\n- Be specific (\\"Save\\" is better than \\"OK\\")\\r\\n\\r\\n### Help Text & Tooltips\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"This is the username field\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Choose a username. You can change this later in Settings.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Add value (don\'t just repeat the label)\\r\\n- Answer the implicit question (\\"What is this?\\" or \\"Why do you need this?\\")\\r\\n- Keep it brief but complete\\r\\n- Link to detailed docs if needed\\r\\n\\r\\n### Empty States\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"No items\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"No projects yet. Create your first project to get started.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Explain why it\'s empty (if not obvious)\\r\\n- Show next action clearly\\r\\n- Make it welcoming, not dead-end\\r\\n\\r\\n### Success Messages\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Success\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Settings saved! Your changes will take effect immediately.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Confirm what happened\\r\\n- Explain what happens next (if relevant)\\r\\n- Be brief but complete\\r\\n- Match the user\'s emotional moment (celebrate big wins)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Loading States\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Loading...\\" (for 30+ seconds)\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Analyzing your data... this usually takes 30-60 seconds\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Set expectations (how long?)\\r\\n- Explain what\'s happening (when it\'s not obvious)\\r\\n- Show progress when possible\\r\\n- Offer escape hatch if appropriate (\\"Cancel\\")\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confirmation Dialogs\\r\\n**Bad**: \\"Are you sure?\\"\\r\\n**Good**: \\"Delete \'Project Alpha\'? This can\'t be undone.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- State the specific action\\r\\n- Explain consequences (especially for destructive actions)\\r\\n- Use clear button labels (\\"Delete project\\" not \\"Yes\\")\\r\\n- Don\'t overuse confirmations (only for risky actions)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Navigation & Wayfinding\\r\\n**Bad**: Generic labels like \\"Items\\" | \\"Things\\" | \\"Stuff\\"\\r\\n**Good**: Specific labels like \\"Your projects\\" | \\"Team members\\" | \\"Settings\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Principles**:\\r\\n- Be specific and descriptive\\r\\n- Use language users understand (not internal jargon)\\r\\n- Make hierarchy clear\\r\\n- Consider information scent (breadcrumbs, current location)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Apply Clarity Principles\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery piece of copy should follow these rules:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Be specific**: \\"Enter email\\" not \\"Enter value\\"\\r\\n2. **Be concise**: Cut unnecessary words (but don\'t sacrifice clarity)\\r\\n3. **Be active**: \\"Save changes\\" not \\"Changes will be saved\\"\\r\\n4. **Be human**: \\"Oops, something went wrong\\" not \\"System error encountered\\"\\r\\n5. **Be helpful**: Tell users what to do, not just what happened\\r\\n6. **Be consistent**: Use same terms throughout (don\'t vary for variety)\\r\\n\\r\\n**NEVER**:\\r\\n- Use jargon without explanation\\r\\n- Blame users (\\"You made an error\\" → \\"This field is required\\")\\r\\n- Be vague (\\"Something went wrong\\" without explanation)\\r\\n- Use passive voice unnecessarily\\r\\n- Write overly long explanations (be concise)\\r\\n- Use humor for errors (be empathetic instead)\\r\\n- Assume technical knowledge\\r\\n- Vary terminology (pick one term and stick with it)\\r\\n- Repeat information (headers restating intros, redundant explanations)\\r\\n- Use placeholders as the only labels (they disappear when users type)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Verify Improvements\\r\\n\\r\\nTest that copy improvements work:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Comprehension**: Can users understand without context?\\r\\n- **Actionability**: Do users know what to do next?\\r\\n- **Brevity**: Is it as short as possible while remaining clear?\\r\\n- **Consistency**: Does it match terminology elsewhere?\\r\\n- **Tone**: Is it appropriate for the situation?\\r\\n\\r\\nRemember: You\'re a clarity expert with excellent communication skills. Write like you\'re explaining to a smart friend who\'s unfamiliar with the product. Be clear, be helpful, be human.\\r\\n"}}'}]

It develops the teaching-content register in [the canonical teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md). That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. The goal is to reproduce those qualities closely through original wording and examples. The central quality is patient, conversational reasoning that the reader can follow and eventually perform.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is a calibration example. This guide separates **observed features** from **instructions for our material**. A source habit is not automatically a rule, a research finding, or permission to import a topic. Matching the voice does not require repeating the same metaphors, anecdotes, exercise sentences, or personal claims.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the part you need\\r\\n\\r\\n- [The evidence and coverage](#the-evidence-and-coverage)\\r\\n- [The voice in one original passage](#the-voice-in-one-original-passage)\\r\\n- [How the teacher relates to the reader](#how-the-teacher-relates-to-the-reader)\\r\\n- [Sentence length and spoken cadence](#sentence-length-and-spoken-cadence)\\r\\n- [Word choice and useful verbal habits](#word-choice-and-useful-verbal-habits)\\r\\n- [Questions that make the reader think](#questions-that-make-the-reader-think)\\r\\n- [Transitions, repetition, metaphor, and emphasis](#transitions-explain-why-the-next-move-follows)\\r\\n- [The complete source progression and depth](#the-complete-source-progression-and-depth)\\r\\n- [What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp](#what-to-carry-into-the-conditional-bootcamp)\\r\\n- [Accuracy and method boundaries](#accuracy-and-method-boundaries)\\r\\n- [Calibration examples and review](#calibration-examples-for-different-lsat-surfaces)\\r\\n- [A reusable writing brief](#a-reusable-writing-brief)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The evidence and coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [source summary](../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) identifies the [preserved HTML](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html), [provenance](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/PROVENANCE.md), and SHA-256. Every supplied section, FAQ entry, table, worked diagram, and drill item was read. HTML line references below refer to that unchanged archived file.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe document has six main sections and six subordinate headings. It ends with six basic drill items and an answer-key reference. One line is explicitly marked partially obscured. The answer key is not supplied. This analysis covers the entire attachment; it cannot reconstruct the missing line or establish the contents of the larger chapter.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML says its formatting was adjusted. We can examine what a pause, table, side note, or separated example does for learning. We cannot claim its font, spacing, color, or CSS exactly reproduces the original publication. No author is identified in the file. The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. Clear teaching can be certain about the limits of what is known.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe teacher does not apologize for asking the reader to think. The explanation makes the request reasonable. In the FAQ, the narrator acknowledges early mistakes and explains the value of practicing anyway. The tone combines patience with a specific demand: attempt the question, write the diagram, inspect the error.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** state the consequence plainly and show why. Preserve legitimate uncertainty. Avoid changing a logical “could” into “must” to make the prose sound stronger. Avoid guarantees about learning outcomes, timing, or score changes unless we have evidence.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Warmth points at the work\\r\\n\\r\\nEncouragement is usually tied to an action. The reader can look back at the lesson, make a provisional attempt, learn from a wrong translation, or build confidence by checking work. The warmth comes from useful help and a teacher who expects progress.\\r\\n\\r\\nUseful form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> If the direction felt unclear, read the statement back in ordinary English. What does it say you need? Keep that complete idea in your diagram.\\r\\n\\r\\nWeak form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You\'ve got this! Conditionals are easy once you know the trick!\\r\\n\\r\\nThe weak version offers reassurance without a way forward and minimizes the actual difficulty.\\r\\n\\r\\n### “I,” “we,” and “you” have different jobs\\r\\n\\r\\n| Pronoun | What it does in the source | Use in our material |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **You** | Gives the reader an action or asks for a decision. | “Try the sentence in the other direction. The rule has already told you what must be true of every parcel with that sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We call the blue sticker the **sufficient condition**. Sufficient means enough. Those extra facts are unnecessary.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Teach a necessary expression through its whole meaning\\r\\n\\r\\n> Editing this newsletter requires an account.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> What does the sentence say the editor needs? **Additional context needed**: quality bar (MVP vs flagship).\\r\\n\\r\\nPerform a meticulous final pass to catch all the small details that separate good work from great work. The difference between shipped and polished.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Design System Discovery\\r\\n\\r\\nAligning the feature to the design system is **not optional**. Polish without alignment is decoration on top of drift, and it makes the next person\'s job harder. Discovery comes before any other polish work.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Find the design system**: Search for design system documentation, component libraries, style guides, or token definitions. Study the core patterns: design principles, target audience, color tokens, spacing scale, typography styles, component API, motion conventions.\\r\\n2. **Note the conventions**: How are shared components imported? What spacing scale is used? Which colors come from tokens vs hard-coded values? What motion and interaction patterns are established? What flow shapes are used for comparable actions (modal vs full-page, inline vs route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit)?\\r\\n3. **Identify drift, then name the root cause**: For every deviation, classify it as a **missing token** (the value should exist in the system but doesn\'t), a **one-off implementation** (a shared component already exists but wasn\'t used), or a **conceptual misalignment** (the feature\'s flow, IA, or hierarchy doesn\'t match neighboring features). The fix differs by category — patch the value, swap to the shared component, or rework the flow. Fixing the symptom without naming the cause is how drift compounds.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf a design system exists, polish **must** align the feature with it. If none exists, polish against the conventions visible in the codebase. **If anything about the system is ambiguous, ask — never guess at design system principles.**\\r\\n\\r\\n## Pre-Polish Assessment\\r\\n\\r\\nUnderstand the current state and goals before touching anything:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Review completeness**:\\r\\n   - Is it functionally complete?\\r\\n   - Are there known issues to preserve (mark with TODOs)?\\r\\n   - What\'s the quality bar? (MVP vs flagship feature?)\\r\\n   - When does it ship? (How much time for polish?)\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Think experience-first**: Who actually uses this, and what\'s the best possible experience for them? Effective design beats decorative polish — a feature that looks beautiful but fights the user\'s flow is not polished. Walk the path from their perspective before opening DevTools.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Identify polish areas**:\\r\\n   - Visual inconsistencies\\r\\n   - Spacing and alignment issues\\r\\n   - Interaction state gaps\\r\\n   - Copy inconsistencies\\r\\n   - Edge cases and error states\\r\\n   - Loading and transition smoothness\\r\\n   - Information architecture and flow drift (does this feature reveal complexity the way neighboring features do?)\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Triage cosmetic vs functional**: Classify each issue as **cosmetic** (looks off, doesn\'t impede the user) or **functional** (breaks, blocks, or confuses the experience). When polish time is tight, functional issues ship first; cosmetic ones can land in a follow-up. Quality should be consistent — never perfect one corner while leaving another rough.\\r\\n\\r\\n**CRITICAL**: Polish is the last step, not the first. Don\'t polish work that\'s not functionally complete.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Polish Systematically\\r\\n\\r\\nWork through these dimensions methodically:\\r\\n\\r\\n### Visual Alignment & Spacing\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Pixel-perfect alignment**: Everything lines up to grid\\r\\n- **Consistent spacing**: All gaps use spacing scale (no random 13px gaps)\\r\\n- **Optical alignment**: Adjust for visual weight (icons may need offset for optical centering)\\r\\n- **Responsive consistency**: Spacing and alignment work at all breakpoints\\r\\n- **Grid adherence**: Elements snap to baseline grid\\r\\n\\r\\n**Check**:\\r\\n- Enable grid overlay and verify alignment\\r\\n- Check spacing with browser inspector\\r\\n- Test at multiple viewport sizes\\r\\n- Look for elements that \\"feel\\" off\\r\\n\\r\\n### Information Architecture & Flow\\r\\n\\r\\nVisual polish on a misshapen flow is wasted work. Match the *shape* of the experience to the system, not just the surface.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Progressive disclosure**: Match how much is revealed when, compared to neighboring features. A settings page exposing 40 fields when the rest of the app reveals 5 at a time is drift, even if every field is perfectly styled.\\r\\n- **Established user flows**: Multi-step actions follow the same shape as comparable flows elsewhere — modal vs full-page, inline edit vs separate route, save-on-blur vs explicit submit, optimistic vs pessimistic updates.\\r\\n- **Hierarchy & complexity**: The same conceptual weight gets the same visual weight throughout. Primary actions don\'t become tertiary in one corner of the product, and tertiary actions don\'t shout.\\r\\n- **Empty, loading, and arrival transitions**: How content arrives, updates, and leaves matches how it does in adjacent features.\\r\\n- **Naming and mental model**: The feature uses the same nouns and verbs as the rest of the system. A \\"Workspace\\" here shouldn\'t be a \\"Project\\" three screens away.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Typography Refinement\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Hierarchy consistency**: Same elements use same sizes/weights throughout\\r\\n- **Line length**: 45-75 characters for body text\\r\\n- **Line height**: Appropriate for font size and context\\r\\n- **Widows & orphans**: No single words on last line\\r\\n- **Hyphenation**: Appropriate for language and column width\\r\\n- **Kerning**: Adjust letter spacing where needed (especially headlines)\\r\\n- **Font loading**: No FOUT/FOIT flashes\\r\\n\\r\\n### Color & Contrast\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Contrast ratios**: All text meets WCAG standards\\r\\n- **Consistent token usage**: No hard-coded colors, all use design tokens\\r\\n- **Theme consistency**: Works in all theme variants\\r\\n- **Color meaning**: Same colors mean same things throughout\\r\\n- **Accessible focus**: Focus indicators visible with sufficient contrast\\r\\n- **Tinted neutrals**: No pure gray or pure black—add subtle color tint (0.01 chroma)\\r\\n- **Gray on color**: Never put gray text on colored backgrounds—use a shade of that color or transparency\\r\\n\\r\\n### Interaction States\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery interactive element needs all states:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Default**: Resting state\\r\\n- **Hover**: Subtle feedback (color, scale, shadow)\\r\\n- **Focus**: Keyboard focus indicator (never remove without replacement)\\r\\n- **Active**: Click/tap feedback\\r\\n- **Disabled**: Clearly non-interactive\\r\\n- **Loading**: Async action feedback\\r\\n- **Error**: Validation or error state\\r\\n- **Success**: Successful completion\\r\\n\\r\\n**Missing states create confusion and broken experiences**.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Micro-interactions & Transitions\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Smooth transitions**: All state changes animated appropriately (150-300ms)\\r\\n- **Consistent easing**: Use ease-out-quart/quint/expo for natural deceleration. Never bounce or elastic—they feel dated.\\r\\n- **No jank**: Smooth animations; use atmospheric blur/filter/mask/shadow effects when they add polish, but bound expensive paint areas and avoid casual layout-property animation\\r\\n- **Appropriate motion**: Motion serves purpose, not decoration\\r\\n- **Reduced motion**: Respects `prefers-reduced-motion`\\r\\n\\r\\n### Content & Copy\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Consistent terminology**: Same things called same names throughout\\r\\n- **Consistent capitalization**: Title Case vs Sentence case applied consistently\\r\\n- **Grammar & spelling**: No typos\\r\\n- **Appropriate length**: Not too wordy, not too terse\\r\\n- **Punctuation consistency**: Periods on sentences, not on labels (unless all labels have them)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Icons & Images\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Consistent style**: All icons from same family or matching style\\r\\n- **Appropriate sizing**: Icons sized consistently for context\\r\\n- **Proper alignment**: Icons align with adjacent text optically\\r\\n- **Alt text**: All images have descriptive alt text\\r\\n- **Loading states**: Images don\'t cause layout shift, proper aspect ratios\\r\\n- **Retina support**: 2x assets for high-DPI screens\\r\\n\\r\\n### Forms & Inputs\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Label consistency**: All inputs properly labeled\\r\\n- **Required indicators**: Clear and consistent\\r\\n- **Error messages**: Helpful and consistent\\r\\n- **Tab order**: Logical keyboard navigation\\r\\n- **Auto-focus**: Appropriate (don\'t overuse)\\r\\n- **Validation timing**: Consistent (on blur vs on submit)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Edge Cases & Error States\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Loading states**: All async actions have loading feedback\\r\\n- **Empty states**: Helpful empty states, not just blank space\\r\\n- **Error states**: Clear error messages with recovery paths\\r\\n- **Success states**: Confirmation of successful actions\\r\\n- **Long content**: Handles very long names, descriptions, etc.\\r\\n- **No content**: Handles missing data gracefully\\r\\n- **Offline**: Appropriate offline handling (if applicable)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Responsiveness\\r\\n\\r\\n- **All breakpoints**: Test mobile, tablet, desktop\\r\\n- **Touch targets**: 44x44px minimum on touch devices\\r\\n- **Readable text**: No text smaller than 14px on mobile\\r\\n- **No horizontal scroll**: Content fits viewport\\r\\n- **Appropriate reflow**: Content adapts logically\\r\\n\\r\\n### Performance\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Fast initial load**: Optimize critical path\\r\\n- **No layout shift**: Elements don\'t jump after load (CLS)\\r\\n- **Smooth interactions**: No lag or jank\\r\\n- **Optimized images**: Appropriate formats and sizes\\r\\n- **Lazy loading**: Off-screen content loads lazily\\r\\n\\r\\n### Code Quality\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Remove console logs**: No debug logging in production\\r\\n- **Remove commented code**: Clean up dead code\\r\\n- **Remove unused imports**: Clean up unused dependencies\\r\\n- **Consistent naming**: Variables and functions follow conventions\\r\\n- **Type safety**: No TypeScript `any` or ignored errors\\r\\n- **Accessibility**: Proper ARIA labels and semantic HTML\\r\\n\\r\\n## Polish Checklist\\r\\n\\r\\nGo through systematically:\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Aligned to the design system (drift named and resolved by root cause)\\r\\n- [ ] Information architecture and flow shape match neighboring features\\r\\n- [ ] Visual alignment perfect at all breakpoints\\r\\n- [ ] Spacing uses design tokens consistently\\r\\n- [ ] Typography hierarchy consistent\\r\\n- [ ] All interactive states implemented\\r\\n- [ ] All transitions smooth (60fps)\\r\\n- [ ] Copy is consistent and polished\\r\\n- [ ] Icons are consistent and properly sized\\r\\n- [ ] All forms properly labeled and validated\\r\\n- [ ] Error states are helpful\\r\\n- [ ] Loading states are clear\\r\\n- [ ] Empty states are welcoming\\r\\n- [ ] Touch targets are 44x44px minimum\\r\\n- [ ] Contrast ratios meet WCAG AA\\r\\n- [ ] Keyboard navigation works\\r\\n- [ ] Focus indicators visible\\r\\n- [ ] No console errors or warnings\\r\\n- [ ] No layout shift on load\\r\\n- [ ] Works in all supported browsers\\r\\n- [ ] Respects reduced motion preference\\r\\n- [ ] Code is clean (no TODOs, console.logs, commented code)\\r\\n\\r\\n**IMPORTANT**: Polish is about details. Zoom in. Squint at it. Use it yourself. The little things add up.\\r\\n\\r\\n**NEVER**:\\r\\n- Polish before it\'s functionally complete\\r\\n- Polish without aligning to the design system — that\'s decoration on drift\\r\\n- Guess at design system principles instead of asking when something is ambiguous\\r\\n- Spend hours on polish if it ships in 30 minutes (triage)\\r\\n- Introduce bugs while polishing (test thoroughly)\\r\\n- Ignore systematic issues (if spacing is off everywhere, fix the system, not just one screen)\\r\\n- Perfect one thing while leaving others rough (consistent quality level)\\r\\n- Create new one-off components when design system equivalents exist\\r\\n- Hard-code values that should use design tokens\\r\\n- Introduce new patterns or flows that diverge from established ones\\r\\n\\r\\n## Final Verification\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore marking as done:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Use it yourself**: Actually interact with the feature\\r\\n- **Test on real devices**: Not just browser DevTools\\r\\n- **Ask someone else to review**: Fresh eyes catch things\\r\\n- **Compare to design**: Match intended design\\r\\n- **Check all states**: Don\'t just test happy path\\r\\n\\r\\n## Clean Up\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter polishing, ensure code quality:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Replace custom implementations**: If the design system provides a component you reimplemented, switch to the shared version.\\r\\n- **Remove orphaned code**: Delete unused styles, components, or files made obsolete by polish.\\r\\n- **Consolidate tokens**: If you introduced new values, check whether they should be tokens.\\r\\n- **Verify DRYness**: Look for duplication introduced during polishing and consolidate.\\r\\n\\r\\nRemember: You have impeccable attention to detail and exquisite taste. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Wall time: 0.0853 seconds\nOutput:'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '## Computer Use\n\nControl native apps and browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.\n\n- Use `cua_repl` (JavaScript) for all UI actions.\n- Do not use other technologies besides `cua_repl` for computer interactions, unless specifically requested by the user (e.g. AppleScript, `osascript`, JXA, System Events, CGEvent synthesis).\n- Prefer a dedicated plugin or skill when it can complete the task; use Computer Use for interactions that are not exposed through a more specific interface.\n- `cua_repl` state is persistent across calls\n- If you create a tab or get an app, the initial UI state is automatically included in the tool result.\n\n## API\n\n```typescript\ntype Vec2 = [x: number, y: number];\ntype ObservationOptions = { emit?: boolean };\ntype StateOptions = ObservationOptions & { disableDiffing?: boolean };\ntype StateAndScreenshot = { state: string; screenshot?: Uint8Array };\ntype PasteOptions = { format?: "text" | "md" | "html" };\ntype ClickOptions = {\n  mouseButton?: MouseButton;\n  clickCount?: number;\n  key?: string;\n  durationMs?: number;\n};\ntype PressKeyOptions = { durationMs?: number };\ntype SelectTextOptions = {\n  prefix?: string;\n  suffix?: string;\n  selectionType?: SelectionType;\n};\ntype Direction = "up" | "down" | "left" | "right" | "u" | "d" | "l" | "r";\ntype SelectionType = "text" | "cursor_before" | "cursor_after";\ntype MouseButton = "left" | "right" | "middle" | "l" | "r" | "m";\n\ninterface Target {\n  getAXState(options?: StateOptions): Promise<string>;\n  getScreenshot(options?: ObservationOptions): Promise<Uint8Array>;\n  getAXStateAndScreenshot(options?: StateOptions): Promise<StateAndScreenshot>;\n  click(target: number | Vec2, options?: ClickOptions): Promise<void>;\n  drag(from: Vec2, to: Vec2): Promise<void>;\n  scroll(target: number | Vec2, direction: Direction, pages?: number): Promise<void>;\n  selectText(elementIndex: number, text: string, options?: SelectTextOptions): Promise<void>;\n  setValue(elementIndex: number, value: string): Promise<void>;\n  performSecondaryAction(elementIndex: number, action: string): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ntype AppInfo = {\n  id: string;\n  displayName?: string;\n  lastUsedDate?: string;\n  useCount?: number;\n  isRunning?: boolean;\n  windows?: WindowInfo[];\n};\ntype WindowInfo = { id: number; app: string; title?: string };\n\ninterface App extends Target {\n  scroll(\n    target: number | Vec2,\n    direction: Direction,\n    distance?: number | { pixels: number },\n  ): Promise<void>;\n  paste(text: string, options?: PasteOptions): Promise<void>;\n  pressKey(key: string, options?: PressKeyOptions): Promise<void>;\n  typeText(text: string): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ntype BrowserInfo = {\n  id: string;\n  name?: string;\n  family?: string;\n  type?: "iab" | "extension" | "cdp" | "mcpapps";\n  profileName?: string;\n  metadata?: { extensionInstanceId?: string; codexSessionId?: string };\n};\n\ntype BrowserTabInfo = {\n  id: string;\n  providerTabId?: string;\n  title?: string;\n  url?: string;\n};\n\ninterface Browser {\n  readonly browserId: string;\n  documentation(): Promise<string>;\n}\n\ninterface BrowserProvider {\n  list(): Promise<BrowserInfo[]>;\n  get(id: string): Promise<Browser>;\n}\n\ninterface BrowserState extends BrowserInfo {\n  tabs: BrowserTabInfo[];\n}\n\ntype TabInfo = {\n  id: string;\n  providerTabId?: string;\n  browserId: string;\n  title?: string;\n  url?: string;\n};\n\ntype State = {\n  apps: AppInfo[];\n  browsers: BrowserState[];\n  errors?: string[]; // Inventory failures; the other inventory remains usable.\n};\n\ntype BrowserOptions = { browser?: string };\ntype GetBrowserOptions = { id?: string; extensionInstanceId?: string; url?: string };\ntype CreateBrowserTabOptions = { visible?: boolean; sessionName?: string };\n\n/** Native input wrappers throw on DOM-only tabs. Use documented Playwright locators instead. */\ninterface Tab extends Target {\n  paste(elementIndex: number | null, text: string, options?: PasteOptions): Promise<void>;\n  pressKey(elementIndex: number | null, key: string, options?: PressKeyOptions): Promise<void>;\n  typeText(elementIndex: number | null, text: string): Promise<void>;\n  readonly id: string;\n  goto?(url: string): Promise<void>;\n  back?(): Promise<void>;\n  forward?(): Promise<void>;\n  reload?(): Promise<void>;\n  close?(): Promise<void>;\n  markDeliverable?(): Promise<void>;\n  markHandoff?(): Promise<void>;\n}\n\ndeclare const cua: {\n  getState(options?: ObservationOptions): Promise<State>;\n  computer: {\n    target: "linux" | "mac" | "windows";\n    launch_app?(input: { app: string }): Promise<void>;\n  };\n\n  getApp(target: string | { windowId: number }): Promise<App>;\n  listApps(options?: ObservationOptions): Promise<AppInfo[]>;\n  listWindows?(options?: ObservationOptions): Promise<WindowInfo[]>;\n\n  /** Select without opening a tab. Use the returned browserId with createBrowserTab. */\n  getBrowser(options?: GetBrowserOptions): Promise<Browser>;\n  /** Apply options before opening the tab; omitted settings stay unchanged, unsupported settings throw. */\n  createBrowserTab(\n    browserId: string,\n    url?: string,\n    options?: CreateBrowserTabOptions,\n  ): Promise<Tab>;\n  /** Bind an existing tab; a string is a tab ID. */\n  getTab(\n    reference: string | { mention: string } | { url: string },\n    options?: BrowserOptions,\n  ): Promise<Tab>;\n  listBrowsers(options?: ObservationOptions): Promise<BrowserInfo[]>;\n  listTabs(options?: BrowserOptions & ObservationOptions): Promise<TabInfo[]>;\n};\n```\n\nMCP App tabs support DOM-based interaction. Use `cua.getTab()` to bind an existing app tab; `createBrowserTab()` cannot create one. Navigation and tab lifecycle methods are optional. Use only methods listed in the returned browser documentation.\n\nFor DOM-only tabs, `getAXState()` uses a DOM snapshot without numeric element indices. `getScreenshot()` uses the tab screenshot API. Disabled observation APIs report an error. Native input wrappers remain present but throw before input. Use the documented Playwright locators to click controls and fill fields.\n\n## Native apps\n\nOn macOS, use `cua.getApp("Example App")` with an app name, path, or bundle ID. On Linux and Windows, use `cua.getApp({ windowId: 123 })` with an exact open window ID from the app inventory. If an app has multiple windows, use their titles to choose the requested one. Do not choose the first window without checking it.\n\n`cua.listWindows()` is available on Linux and Windows and includes open windows that have no app entry. If the requested app has no open window, launch its inventory ID with `await cua.computer.launch_app({ app: appId })`, then refresh the inventory and select a window. `getApp` does not launch apps on Linux or Windows.\n\nLinux input stays bound to the selected window. Sky sends it without activating that window or moving the desktop pointer. The app can still activate a new window or grab the pointer during a held click, drag, or menu interaction. Coordinates are relative to the selected window. Windows input activates the selected window. Get a fresh Windows screenshot before coordinate actions. The bound app uses that screenshot\'s coordinate mapping until the next observation; an AX-only observation clears it.\n\nLinux app coordinate clicks support `durationMs`, a non-negative safe integer giving the milliseconds\nto hold the mouse button down for each click. For example,\n`await app.click([640, 360], { mouseButton: "right", durationMs: 2000 })` holds the right button for\ntwo seconds before releasing it. The same option works for left clicks and keeps the existing\nbound-window routing. Timed Linux clicks require window-relative coordinates, not an element index.\n`performSecondaryAction` invokes a named accessibility action; it does not provide a timed\nmouse-button press.\n\nLinux app coordinate clicks also support `key`, a key chord held during the mouse click using the\nsame format as `pressKey`. For example, `await app.click([640, 360], { key: "shift" })` performs\nShift+left-click. The chord is released between clicks and can be combined with `durationMs`.\nLinux clicks with `key` require window-relative coordinates. Windows native apps reject `key`\nand `durationMs` options.\n\n## Workflow\n\nAfter performing one or more UI actions, call `getAXState()` before deciding what to do next. This keeps you in the current UI state and forces you to re-derive fresh element indices from the latest accessibility text instead of reusing stale ones.\nFor token efficiency, when appropriate, the accessibility tree will be returned as a diff from the most previous accessibility tree, listing only the elements that were removed, added, or changed. Prefer this default diff output; pass `{ disableDiffing: true }` only when you need a fresh full accessibility tree. After a screenshot-only observation, request a full tree before relying on accessibility indexes again.\nLinux and Windows always return full accessibility state. Linux reports the tree source. `at_spi` elements support the actions listed in the tree; `x11` fallback elements are observation-only, so use a screenshot and window-relative coordinates for input.\nMinimize model and tool round trips while retaining fresh UI state:\n\n- Batch deterministic actions and the resulting `getAXState()` into one call. You may interact with the UI and return the updated state in that same call, so this does not require a separate tool call.\n- Calling `cua.getApp(...)`, `cua.getTab(...)`, and `cua.createBrowserTab(...)` returns app or tab bindings and automatically displays the latest AX state after they run.\n- For `chrome://newtab` (with or without a trailing slash) and Orbit’s signed new-tab extension page, `cua.getTab(...)` displays tab metadata without reading or changing the new-tab page. Use the returned tab\'s `goto(url)` to navigate to an allowed website.\n- If a standalone `getAXState()` reports no accessibility-tree change, do not immediately repeat it without an intervening action. Use `getScreenshot()`, `getAXStateAndScreenshot()`, or `{ disableDiffing: true }` only when you can identify missing context that representation should provide.\n- Prefer a directly relevant result already visible in the current state over opening broader intermediate UI such as “Show All.”\n- Once the requested result is visibly present, stop exploring and respond.\n  Perform one or more actions, and then fetch the latest state:\n\n```typescript\nawait target.click(42);\nawait target.setValue(42, "openai.com");\nawait tab.typeText(42, "hello");\nawait tab.pressKey(42, "Return");\nawait target.scroll(42, "down", 1);\nawait target.scroll([640, 480], "down", 1);\nawait target.selectText(42, "hello");\nawait target.performSecondaryAction(42, "Expand");\nawait target.getAXState();\n```\n\n## Output\n\n- For text output, use `nodeRepl.write(...)`. The API accepts strings and other values. Use `JSON.stringify(...)` when you want JSON.\n- For image output, use `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)`. The API accepts data or file URLs, PNG/JPEG/WebP bytes, or `{ bytes, mimeType }`.\n- The following APIs output their result internally, calling `nodeRepl.write(...)` and/or `nodeRepl.emitImage(...)` will duplicate the output: `getAXState()`, `getScreenshot()`, `getAXStateAndScreenshot()`, `cua.getState()`, `cua.getApp(...)`, `cua.getTab(...)`, `cua.createBrowserTab(...)`, `cua.listApps()`, `cua.listBrowsers()`, and `cua.listTabs()`. Pass `{ emit: false }` to observation and discovery methods to disable their result output. First-use documentation is still displayed. `cua.getBrowser()` automatically displays its first-use documentation; do not write the returned browser object or reread its documentation.\n- `cua.listWindows()` also displays its result unless `emit: false`. Windows screenshot methods always display images through Sky and reject `emit: false` before capture. They also reject a result with multiple screenshot regions because the bound API returns one image. Sky displays those regions before the error.\n\n## Notes\n\n- For browser tabs, `typeText`, `paste`, and `pressKey` take an optional element index as their first argument and focus that element before sending input. Pass `null` to use the currently focused element.\n- For efficiency, prefer element index based actions over coordinate actions whenever an accessibility element is available. For native apps and tabs that support coordinate input, use screenshots and coordinates when AX actions fail. For DOM-only tabs, use Playwright locators. You can also get a screenshot if you need visual context.\n- macOS app `paste` uses the system pasteboard then restores the user\'s previous clipboard contents. Linux and Windows app `paste` support only `text` and use the platform\'s native text input. Browser `paste` does not restore clipboard contents, and its `md` format inserts Markdown source as plain text. Specify `text`, `md`, or `html` explicitly where supported. Prefer `paste` for formatted content and multiline text.\n- Native app `scroll` accepts a page count on macOS. On Linux, omit the distance for the native default or pass `{ pixels: 500 }`. On Windows, pass a coordinate target and `{ pixels: 500 }`; element targets and page counts are unsupported. Linux element clicks support one left or right click. Use coordinates for other click options.\n- `selectText` is unavailable on Linux and Windows. `setValue` is unavailable on Linux. These methods throw before sending input. Use the supported bound actions to edit the UI and verify the result.\n- If the UI is not behaving as expected, try fetching the latest `getAXState()` to make sure you have the latest context.\n- `performSecondaryAction()` is for invoking an accessibility action that an element exposes besides a normal click, such as expanding a disclosure row, showing a menu, incrementing a control, or cancelling something. It requires an action actually exposed for that element in the accessibility text. Do not guess action names.\n- `selectText()` selects matching text in an editable element. Use `prefix` and `suffix` to disambiguate repeated matches, and `selectionType` to choose whether to select the text itself or place the cursor before or after it.\n- `pressKey()` presses a key or key combination, including modifier and navigation keys. It supports xdotool-style key syntax. Examples: `"a"`, `"Return"`, `"Tab"`, `"super+c"`, `"Up"`, and `"KP_0"` for numpad `0`.\n- `click` holds each mouse press for `durationMs`; macOS apps and browser tabs hold `key` across the full click sequence.\n- On macOS, `cua.getApp(...)` accepts an app\'s display name, full app path, or bundle identifier and launches the app in the background if needed. If display-name resolution fails, retry with the app\'s bundle identifier from `cua.listApps()`.\n- `getAXState()`, `getScreenshot()` and `getAXStateAndScreenshot()` automatically wait an appropriate amount of time before capturing new state. In order to complete the task as quickly as possible, don’t pause or delay (ex: `setTimeout(...)`) before getting UI state. Instead, rely on the internal wait.\n\nPersist until the request is fully completed end-to-end. Attempting an action is not completion: verify that the returned UI state visibly shows the requested result. If an action leaves the state unchanged, produces no results, or only reaches an intermediate page, try another approach.
