| Operator brain (how to think about automation) | `references/3ms-framework.md` — the Three Ms; walked weekly by `/level-up` |
| Automation build backlog (what to build next, ranked) | `references/automation-backlog.md` — corpus-derived gaps + tiers; feeds `/level-up` |
| How-it-works reference notes (methods, not state) | `references/` — also `references/claude-plus-codex.md`, `references/obsidian-command-center.md`, `references/second-brain-levels.md` |
| Web research and Firecrawl agents | `references/firecrawl.md` (guidelines in `references/firecrawl/`) |
| Shared Windows CLI tools for Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity | `references/ai-workspace/windows-cli-toolchain.md` — installed paths, PATH refresh, and usage for `uv`, `yt-dlp`, FFmpeg, and Deno |
| Immutable source evidence · intake queue | `raw/sources/` · `raw/inbox/` — one inbox, one archive |
| Archived web clips, with provenance + hashes | `raw/sources/clips/<slug>/` — clip + `PROVENANCE.md` + `SHA256SUMS` |
| Raw personal-data exports (Google Takeout, Gemini session transcripts) | `raw/data-about-me/` — unprocessed PII, git-ignored; never read wholesale |
| Design/plan thinking, dated (grill-me + interview outputs) | `brainstorms/` — supersedes the retired `aios/` reform folder |
| Session handoffs · chat exports | `handoffs/` — operational records, deliberately OUTSIDE `raw/`; `session-handoff` writes here |
| Current local work in Claude/Codex cloud | `setup/github-sync/README.md`; private `codex/local-sync/<machine>/<checkout>` branches and generated `.cloud-sync/` metadata/conversation exports. Cloud edits use separate task branches. |
| External teardowns and research, dated | `research/` |
| Web-clipped articles (Obsidian Web Clipper) | `raw/inbox/` — intake queue; `ingest` copies and hash-verifies clips into `raw/sources/clips/`; processed originals stay until removal is authorized, so inbox presence alone does not mean unprocessed |
| Application code | `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/` — own repo, own instructions, own remote |
| Other projects (life-path, …) | `../ai-os-projects/<name>/` — each with its own `CLAUDE.md` + `.claude/` |

Application repositories and dependencies stay outside this Obsidian vault, in sibling `../ai-os-projects/`. Do not create a junction from the vault back into that directory.

## Retrieval order

1. `wiki/hot.md` — current-session narrative and open threads.
2. `wiki/index.md` → the page (teaching knowledge: `corpus/index.md`; a student: their folder). Follow links; there is no semantic search and none is needed at this size.
3. The live system — the final freshness escalation.

**Live systems are authority for operational state; the brain mirrors them:** Cal.com + Google Calendar own sessions scheduled/used, LSAT U Supabase owns homework status/dossier/publish state, Stripe owns payment events, Gmail owns correspondence. On any disagreement, the backend wins. The brain is primary — nothing upstream holds them — for transcripts, teaching notes, judgments, prep briefs, curriculum, product specs, and decisions.

**Do not read the wiki unless the task needs it.** Retrieval costs context every turn. Skip it for: code edits in `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/`; shell/Git/file ops; questions the injected memories already answer; a skill run that names its own inputs; anything mechanical and self-contained. Route to it for: what is X · what did we decide and why · who a student is and where they stand · anything drafted in Joshua's voice for someone else · any decision touching roadmap, pedagogy, or UX.

**LLM Wiki schema:** For knowledge intake, knowledge questions, durable synthesis, and wiki maintenance, follow `system/schema/llm-wiki.md`. Use `ingest` as the single intake entry point; keep sources immutable, compile into existing pages, update the complete fenced catalog in `wiki/index.md`, and append changes to `wiki/log.md`. Preserve domain homes and live-system authority. Mechanical tasks retain the retrieval exceptions above.

**Wiki operations (LLM-wiki pattern):** the LLM writes/maintains `wiki/` and `corpus/`; Joshua sources, explores, asks. Raw sources are immutable — read, never modify. *Ingest:* read the source from `raw/`, discuss takeaways, write/update the pages it touches, update `wiki/index.md`, append to `wiki/log.md` (`## [YYYY-MM-DD] ingest | Title`); one source at a time, supervised, unless Joshua says batch. *Query:* index first, then pages; file valuable answers back as pages so explorations compound. *Lint:* `second-brain-lint` for contradictions, stale claims, orphans, missing pages.

## Voice

- **No em-dashes, ever.** Joshua never types them; a stray em-dash reads as AI and costs trust.
- **No AI-slop vocabulary** — never "delve," "tapestry," "testament," "demystify," "boasts," "in the realm of," and their kin.
- **Anything a student or prospect will read** routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md` and is drafted, never sent, unless it is a pre-approved template.
- **LSAT teaching:** use project-owned `lsat-u-voice` and `references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md`; this Joshua-selected standard takes precedence over older vendor voice blends.
- **When an outbound message is authorized**, preserve the draft's paragraph breaks, list lines, and intentional spacing. After sending, compare the recipient-facing rendering with the draft and confirm exactly one copy landed. Report any mismatch; never resend automatically.
- **Lead with your recommendation, not a menu.** Be decisive; don't over-hedge.
- **Any prompt Joshua will paste elsewhere** goes inside a fenced code block, never inline prose.

## Tools, keys, and secrets

- **The entire secret model is `.env` + `.gitignore`.** The root `.env` (git-ignored — verify with `git check-ignore .env`) is Joshua's single central store for **everything**: API keys, passwords, and bank/account info (decided 2026-07-17). OAuth client secrets live in `~/.config/gws/`, outside the repo. There is no vault, no Keychain, no encrypted store (`records.sparsebundle` is dead) and none is wanted. Never paste a credential into chat — add it to `.env` directly in the editor.
- **Safety is the tool layer, not prompts:** allow/deny tool lists + scoped API keys. Jay 2 acts under its own credentials and never impersonates Joshua.
- **Connected live systems:** Cal.com, Google Calendar, LSAT U Supabase, Stripe, Gmail. Full registry in `connections.md`.
- **Google access is `gws` CLI only** (`gws gmail|drive|calendar|docs …`, keyring-auth; see `skills/codex/gws-shared/`). Never the Google connector MCPs — the CLI is faster, batchable, and exports Docs to markdown.
- **Shared Windows command tools:** use `uv`, `yt-dlp`, `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe`, `ffplay`, and `deno` from the Windows user PATH. For versions, locations, how to invoke them, or a stale terminal environment, read `references/ai-workspace/windows-cli-toolchain.md`. Check before reinstalling; restart the affected IDE when its inherited PATH is stale.
- **Government IDs stay outside this OS.** Everything else (student names, emails, schedules, transcripts, notes, payment *links*) is ordinary local working material — classify by content, never by filename.
- **Git remote is enabled.** `origin` is GitHub (`vnjkoxpl-42905/ai-os`, decided 2026-09-29). The outer repo never tracks `.env`, `../ai-os-projects/lsatu/` (own repo), runtime logs, or locks. Do not create gitlinks.
- **New laptop restore:** GitHub contains tracked ai-os files and skills. It deliberately excludes `.env`, `raw/`, app repos, credentials, and machine sessions. Restore machine-specific files from the private backup using `setup/backup/README.md` and its `README - START HERE.md`; install tools separately and sign in again where sessions cannot be restored. Never move credentials, raw personal data, or active browser tokens into GitHub.
- **Authorized cloud transfer (2026-10-07):** private sync branches also carry portable skills, memory and conversation exports. Joshua explicitly authorized credential transfer; implementation uses the authenticated encrypted package described in `setup/github-sync/README.md`; plaintext secrets and its unlock key stay outside GitHub and Drive. Cloud authentication and native browser sessions still require separate verification.

## Skills

Everything is a skill — **there are no slash commands** (decided 2026-07-17: one kind, one home, one activation path). The catalog at `skills/` and `agents/` is inert storage; nothing auto-loads. An item runs only once **activated by copy** (not symlink) into `.agents/skills/` (Claude: `.claude/skills/`). Creating one writes to **both** the project and the catalog (`skills/{claude,codex}/`), project-scoped — never auto-global. `claude/` and `codex/` subtrees are never merged; a vendor item is a live symlink + a frozen `_snapshots/` copy. `system/scripts/check-skills.sh` validates the model; `skills/INDEX.md` indexes it.

Active in this root. Run `pickup` only when Joshua explicitly asks for it. Do not run it automatically at session start. Use `wrapup` at the end of substantive sessions:

| Skill | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pickup` / `wrapup` | `pickup` only on Joshua's explicit request / `wrapup` at session end (wrapup persists to the wiki ledgers) |
| `session-handoff` | mid-work context reset near ~250k, or passing work Codex↔Claude — chat-only, writes nothing |
| `audit` | scoring the OS against the Four Cs (structural health, /100) |
| `level-up` | weekly 3Ms interview to find + ship one automation |
| `consultation-inquiry-drafts`, `-followup-drafts`, `inbound-tutoring-replies` | drafting to prospects/students — always via the teaching voice |
| `guided-drill-assignment` | assigning a student a drill |
| `lsat-u-platform-actions` | doing anything ON lsatprep.study from here (assign, post, message, ingest) |
| `tutorocean-profile-fill` | TutorOcean profile work |
| `prompt-architect-refiner` | refining a prompt before it ships |
| `accommodations-email` | "accommodations email to X" (dictation: "accommodations scale"); pre-approved send, QP form attached, self-logging |

When a skill run exposes a gap, improve the skill before moving on. Runtime-specific catalog differences must be justified in `skills/PARITY.md`; undeclared differences are defects.

## Guardrails

- **95% rule.** Make no changes until you are 95% confident what Joshua wants. Ask until you are.
- **Lovable credits require confirmation.** Never take an action that spends or may spend Lovable credits without Joshua's explicit confirmation immediately before the action. Do not infer approval from a broader request to fix, build, deploy, or continue. Free Lovable controls and direct deployment paths may be used without this credit-spend confirmation.
- **Lovable Cloud deploys through Lovable.** LSAT U currently uses a Lovable Cloud-managed backend. Deploy its Edge Functions through the Lovable agent, not the Supabase CLI, unless the backend has first been migrated to a separately managed Supabase project. Confirm this route with Joshua before starting a Lovable deployment.
- **Root stays thin.** Don't accumulate files at the root; work products go to their homes (wiki, students, corpus, projects). Anything left at root gets filed before the session ends.
- **Delegate bulk work.** Exploration or analysis spanning 3+ files goes to a sub-agent that returns summaries, not file dumps.
- **Shell ergonomics.** Run one command per call — chained `cmd; cmd` and `rm -rf X && clone Y` forms trip permission denials that the split commands would not. Never poll with `sleep`. Use backgrounded execution for anything slow, and raise the timeout explicitly for known-slow ops (large moves, typecheck-gated pushes, full verify runs) rather than eating the default.
- **Search before creating.** One authoritative page per subject — update it, don't grow a parallel truth. `wiki/index.md` catalogs every page and updates on every ingest.
- **Preserve provenance and source hashes.** Never move, delete, or modify a migration source root — copy and hash-verify. Never follow a source symlink outside its registered root.
- **Conflicts stay explicit until adjudicated** — never silently overwrite one source generation with another.
- **Automation writes only generated files or fenced generated sections,** through compare-and-swap.
- **Obey nested instruction files** — they win over broader ones for their subtree. LSATU's recovered `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` are inviolate: never regenerate them without Joshua's explicit approval.
- **Memory = native automemory.** "Remember that…" writes one fact per file to the native store; `MEMORY.md` indexes it. This file is the rules; memory is learned facts — never mix them. Transcripts and raw captures never auto-promote.
- **Append meaningful system changes** to `wiki/log.md`; log locked decisions to `decisions/log.md`.

## Dual-runtime (Codex + Claude)

- Begin at the Git-root `AGENTS.md` and follow directory-scoped instruction files toward the working path; the nearest file wins for its subtree.
- Keep root instructions inside the runtime byte budget. Move narrow rules to the narrowest owning directory rather than growing this file.
- Activated skills are **copies** in `.agents/skills/` (from `skills/codex/`); agent definitions convert to `.codex/agents/*.toml` with the instructions in `developer_instructions`.
- Claude reads `CLAUDE.md` and never this file. Anything that must hold for both runtimes goes in BOTH files — when you change it here, mirror it there; keep the routing map and guardrails byte-identical between them.
- Activation is unequal by design: Codex reads copies in `.agents/skills/`, Claude reads copies in `.claude/skills/`. Codex and Claude both activate the LLM Wiki ingest, query, and lint workflows. Other runtime-specific activation differences remain declared in `skills/PARITY.md`. Never have separate runtimes writing the same page concurrently.
- Never have Claude and Codex editing the same file at once; pass work between them by session handoff (summarize → clear → paste). At ~250k tokens, hand off rather than riding autocompact.

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 4.0 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"06afbf","wall_time_seconds":0.6614131,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2317,"output":"---\\r\\ntitle: Teaching Voice\\r\\ntype: concept\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, content]\\r\\ncreated: 2026-06-10\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nstatus: active\\r\\nsubject: Teaching Voice\\r\\naliases: []\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Teaching Voice\\r\\n\\r\\nHow LSAT U sounds, across every surface. This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**LSAT teaching standard, selected 2026-10-02:** Joshua chose the supplied Conditional Reasoning transcription as the reference for how LSAT material should sound and unfold. Read [LSAT teaching voice standard](../references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md) before drafting lessons, notes, explanations, drills, flashcards, quizzes, or instructional feedback. It contains the detailed source analysis, original calibration examples, progression, and review rubric. [Source identity and limits](sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) are preserved separately. This choice develops the teaching-content register below; correspondence and marketing retain their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Air between ideas. Real correspondence is short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters). In teaching, vary sentence and paragraph length with the reasoning: give an explanation room, then let a short sentence settle the consequence. Do not impose email brevity on a lesson or cut its intermediate reasoning.\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\"; \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs: never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n\\r\\nVerbatim-grounded reference lines for the situations that recur most. Adapt, never paste blindly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Student reschedules / cancels:** low-pressure, no guilt.\\r\\n  > No worries at all. It happens, so please don\'t worry about it. If you would like to reschedule, just let me know.\\r\\n- **He missed / no-showed (approved make-good template):** full ownership, real reason, offer to make it right (see the apology move above). When the cause was an unexpected health issue, the approved shape is: sincerely apologize, state that a serious health scare unexpectedly took him out of commission, offer a **completely free, full LSAT session**, and hand them the complimentary booking link `https://cal.com/joshua-jtx5ud/complimentary-session`. Emphasis stays limited: bold the complimentary offer, italicize the line that one focused session can put points on the board. Draft in Gmail; never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.\\r\\n- **Consultation reminder (day-of):**\\r\\n  > Just checking in before our consultation today. Looking forward to speaking with you. I just wanted to make sure everything is still good.\\r\\n- **Consultation follow-up:** warm, specific to their situation.\\r\\n  > Really nice meeting you. I enjoyed our conversation ... I\'m glad we got to talk through where you\'re at and what you\'re aiming for on test day.\\r\\n- **Inbound prospect (hasn\'t booked):** state availability plainly, no overselling, hand them the next step.\\r\\n  > Thanks for reaching out ... I\'d be happy to talk more about what you\'re working on and see if we\'d be a good fit. You can schedule a consultation here.\\r\\n- **Student under real-life stress:** meet the person first.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"c3a4d0","wall_time_seconds":0.4226104,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":2794,"output":"import { useEffect, useRef, useState, type ReactNode } from \'react\';\\r\\nimport { Link } from \'react-router-dom\';\\r\\nimport { ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, BookOpen, Bookmark, Dumbbell, Menu, Sparkles } from \'lucide-react\';\\r\\nimport { PageHeader } from \'@/bootcamps/main-conclusion/components/primitives/PageHeader\';\\r\\nimport { Sheet, SheetContent, SheetTitle, SheetTrigger } from \'@/components/ui/sheet\';\\r\\nimport { OPENING_COURSE_PATH, openingCourseStep, type OpeningCourseStep } from \'../openingCoursePath\';\\r\\nimport { OpeningCourseContent } from \'./OpeningCourseContent\';\\r\\nimport { StudyDeck } from \'./StudyDeck\';\\r\\nimport \'./opening-course.css\';\\r\\n\\r\\nexport type OpeningCourseUrl = (destination: string, run?: boolean) => string;\\r\\n\\r\\nconst practiceSaveNotice = \\"Practice answers aren\'t saved to your account. Reloading or leaving the course clears them.\\";\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function OpeningCourseNavigation({ view, url }: { view: string; url: OpeningCourseUrl }) {\\r\\n  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);\\r\\n  const focusDestination = useRef(false);\\r\\n  function closeForNavigation() { focusDestination.current = open; setOpen(false); }\\r\\n  const navigation = <nav aria-label=\\"Conditional course\\">\\r\\n    <p>Intro path</p><Link aria-current={view === \'lessons\' || !!openingCourseStep(view) ? \'page\' : undefined} to={url(\'lessons\')} onClick={closeForNavigation}><BookOpen size={18}/>Lessons</Link>\\r\\n    <p>Practice</p><Link aria-current={view === \'practice\' ? \'page\' : undefined} to={url(\'practice\')} onClick={closeForNavigation}><Sparkles size={18}/>Practice Drills</Link>\\r\\n    <Link aria-current={view === \'labs\' ? \'page\' : undefined} to={url(\'labs\')} onClick={closeForNavigation}><Dumbbell size={18}/>Drill Lab</Link>\\r\\n    <p>Tools</p><Link aria-current={view === \'tools\' ? \'page\' : undefined} to={url(\'tools\')} onClick={closeForNavigation}><Bookmark size={18}/>Flashcards</Link>\\r\\n  </nav>;\\r\\n  return <>\\r\\n    <aside className=\\"oc-course-rail\\"><Link className=\\"oc-back\\" to=\\"/classroom\\"><ArrowLeft size={15}/>Classroom</Link><div className=\\"oc-brand\\">Conditional logic</div>{navigation}</aside>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"oc-mobile-nav\\"><Link to={url(\'lessons\')}>Conditional logic</Link><Sheet open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}><SheetTrigger asChild><button type=\\"button\\"><Menu size={18}/>Course menu</button></SheetTrigger><SheetContent side=\\"left\\" className=\\"oc-course-drawer\\" aria-describedby={undefined} onCloseAutoFocus={event => {\\r\\n      if (!focusDestination.current) return;\\r\\n      event.preventDefault();\\r\\n      focusDestination.current = false;\\r\\n      requestAnimationFrame(() => {\\r\\n        const heading = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(\'.oc-course-screen [data-course-heading] h1\');\\r\\n        if (heading) { heading.tabIndex = -1; heading.focus({ preventScroll: true }); }\\r\\n      });\\r\\n    }}><SheetTitle>Conditional logic</SheetTitle>{navigation}</SheetContent></Sheet></div>\\r\\n  </>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction CourseCard({ step, url }: { step: OpeningCourseStep; url: OpeningCourseUrl }) {\\r\\n  return <li className=\\"oc-path-card\\"><span className=\\"oc-label\\">{step.type}</span><h2>{step.title}</h2><p>{step.description}</p><Link className=\\"oc-action\\" to={url(step.id)}>{step.type === \'note\' ? <BookOpen size={16}/> : <Dumbbell size={16}/>} {step.type === \'note\' ? \'Read lesson\' : \'View drill\'}<ArrowRight size={16}/></Link></li>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nconst drillInstructions: Record<string, { summary: string; heading: string; steps: string[] }> = {\\r\\n  \'foundation-practice\': {\\r\\n    summary: \'Fresh rules and cases\', heading: \'Decide what follows\',\\r\\n    steps: [\'Read the rule and the facts supplied with it.\', \'Decide what follows, what is required, and what the information leaves open.\', \'Check the explanation. If your answer needs changing, try the case again.\'],\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  \'sufficient-practice\': {\\r\\n    summary: \'Condition targets and diagrams\', heading: \'Find the whole sufficient condition\',\\r\\n    steps: [\'Find the complete idea the sufficient expression refers to.\', \'Put that condition on the left and the required condition on the right. Read the arrow back in English.\', \'Check your work, then build a possible case that shows why the reverse does not follow.\'],\\r\\n  },\\r\\n  \'contrapositive-practice\': {\\r\\n    summary: \'Originals and contrapositives\', heading: \'Keep both diagrams tied to the sentence\',\\r\\n    steps: [\'Identify the indicator and both complete conditions, including any negatives.\', \'Build the original diagram. Reverse the sides and negate both conditions to form its contrapositive.\', \'Read both diagrams in English before checking. Use the explanation to repair any change in meaning.\'],\\r\\n  },\\r\\n};\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction DrillEntry({ step, url }: { step: OpeningCourseStep; url: OpeningCourseUrl }) {\\r\\n  if (step.id === \'mixed-practice\') return <div className=\\"oc-drill-landing oc-translation-entry\\">\\r\\n    <div className=\\"oc-drill-overview\\">\\r\\n      <Link className=\\"oc-back oc-entry-back\\" to={url(\'lessons\')}><ArrowLeft size={16}/>Back to lessons</Link>\\r\\n      <header data-course-heading><p className=\\"oc-label\\">Conditional reasoning</p><h1>{step.title}</h1><p>{step.description}</p></header>\\r\\n    </div>\\r\\n    <section className=\\"oc-drill-start\\" aria-label=\\"Practice instructions\\">\\r\\n      <h2>One step at a time</h2>\\r\\n      <p>Before each section, we\'ll show you what to look for. Then you\'ll put it into practice.</p>\\r\\n      <Link className=\\"oc-action oc-start-pulse\\" to={url(step.id, true)}>Start practice<ArrowRight size={16}/></Link>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"oc-save-scope\\">{practiceSaveNotice}</p>\\r\\n    </section>\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n  const instructions = drillInstructions[step.id];\\r\\n  return <div className=\\"oc-drill-landing\\">\\r\\n    <div className=\\"oc-drill-overview\\"><Link className=\\"oc-back\\" to={url(\'lessons\')}><ArrowLeft size={16}/>Back to lessons</Link>\\r\\n      <header data-course-heading><h1>{step.title}</h1><p>{step.description}</p></header>\\r\\n    </div>\\r\\n    <section className=\\"oc-drill-start\\" aria-label=\\"Practice instructions\\">\\r\\n      <p className=\\"oc-label\\">{instructions.summary}</p><h2>{instructions.heading}</h2>\\r\\n      <ol>{instructions.steps.map(instruction => <li key={instruction}>{instruction}</li>)}</ol>\\r\\n      <Link className=\\"oc-action\\" to={url(step.id, true)}>Start practice<ArrowRight size={16}/></Link>\\r\\n    </section>\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function OpeningCourseScreen({ view = \'lessons\', run = false, url, steps = OPENING_COURSE_PATH, recordedPractice }: {\\r\\n  view?: string; run?: boolean; url: OpeningCourseUrl; steps?: OpeningCourseStep[]; recordedPractice?: ReactNode;\\r\\n}) {\\r\\n  const current = steps.find(step => step.id === view);\\r\\n  const [visited, setVisited] = useState<string[]>([]);\\r\\n  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);\\r\\n  useEffect(() => {\\r\\n    if (current && (current.type === \'note\' || run)) setVisited(prior => prior.includes(view) ? prior : [...prior, view]);\\r\\n    requestAnimationFrame(() => {\\r\\n      const heading = root.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(\'[data-course-heading] h1\');\\r\\n      if (heading) heading.tabIndex = -1;\\r\\n      heading?.focus({ preventScroll: true });\\r\\n      const arrival = root.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>(current?.type === \'drill\' && run ? \'.oc-drill-run-header\' : \'[data-course-heading]\');\\r\\n      arrival?.scrollIntoView?.({ block: \'start\', behavior: \'instant\' });\\r\\n    });\\r\\n  }, [view, run, current]);\\r\\n  const index = steps.findIndex(step => step.id === view);\\r\\n  const prior = steps[index - 1];\\r\\n  const next = steps[index + 1];\\r\\n  const list = view === \'labs\' || view === \'practice\' ? steps.filter(step => step.type === \'drill\') : steps;\\r\\n  const isIndex = [\'lessons\', \'labs\', \'practice\'].includes(view);\\r\\n  return <div ref={root} className=\\"oc-course-screen\\">\\r\\n    {isIndex && <div className=\\"oc-course-index\\">\\r\\n      <div data-course-heading><PageHeader noBloom eyebrow={view === \'lessons\' ? \'Introduction\' : \'Practice\'} title={view === \'lessons\' ? \'Conditional reasoning.\' : view === \'labs\' ? \'Make the move yourself.\' : \'Practice the reasoning.\'} description={view === \'lessons\' ? \'Learn one idea, use it, then build on it. The drills between lessons give you a chance to test the meaning before moving on.\' : \'Make an attempt before reading the explanation. Name the mistake, repair it and try again.\'}/></div>\\r\\n      {view === \'practice\' && recordedPractice}\\r\\n      <ol className=\\"oc-course-path\\">{list.map(step => <CourseCard key={step.id} step={step} url={url}/>)}</ol>\\r\\n      {!list.length && <p>No opening lessons are available in this work.</p>}\\r\\n    </div>}\\r\\n    {view === \'tools\' && <div className=\\"oc-course-note\\">\\r\\n      <div data-course-heading><PageHeader noBloom eyebrow=\\"Tools\\" title=\\"Recall before you turn.\\" description=\\"Say the relationship in your own words. Turn the card to compare your reasoning.\\"/></div>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"co-opening\\">{steps.some(step => step.unitId === \'orientation\' || step.unitId === \'sufficient-necessary\') && <><h2>Enough and required</h2><StudyDeck group=\\"foundation\\"/></>}{steps.some(step => step.unitId === \'group-1\') && <><h2>Sufficient-condition words</h2><StudyDeck group=\\"group-1\\"/></>}{steps.some(step => step.unitId === \'group-2\') && <><h2>Necessary-condition words</h2><StudyDeck group=\\"group-2\\"/></>}{!steps.length && <p>No flashcards are available in this work.</p>}</div>\\r\\n    </div>}\\r\\n    {current?.type === \'drill\' && !run && <DrillEntry step={current} url={url}/>}\\r\\n    {current && (current.type === \'note\' || run) && <div className={current.type === \'note\' ? \'oc-course-note\' : \'oc-drill-run-header\'}>\\r\\n      <div data-course-heading>{current.type === \'note\' ? <header className=\\"mb-10\\">\\r\\n        <h1 className=\\"font-mc-serif text-ink leading-[0.94] italic text-[clamp(3.1rem,7vw,6rem)] font-medium tracking-[-0.06em]\\">{current.title}</h1>\\r\\n        <p className=\\"font-mc-sans text-body-prose mt-4 text-ink-soft max-w-[60ch] leading-relaxed\\">{current.description}</p>\\r\\n      </header> : <header><p className=\\"oc-label\\">Practice</p><h1>{current.title}</h1></header>}</div>\\r\\n      {current.type === \'drill\' && <Link className=\\"oc-back oc-drill-back\\" to={url(view)}><ArrowLeft size={16}/>Back to instructions</Link>}\\r\\n      {current.id === \'mixed-practice\' && <p className=\\"oc-save-scope\\">{practiceSaveNotice}</p>}\\r\\n    </div>}\\r\\n    <div className=\\"oc-course-bodies\\">{steps.filter(step => visited.includes(step.id)).map(step => <div key={step.id} hidden={step.id !== view || (step.type === \'drill\' && !run)} className=\\"oc-course-body co-opening cr-sequence\\"><OpeningCourseContent id={step.id}/></div>)}</div>\\r\\n    {current && (current.type === \'note\' || run) && <nav className=\\"oc-course-turn\\" aria-label=\\"Course navigation\\">{prior ? <Link to={url(prior.id)}><span>Previous {prior.type === \'note\' ? \'lesson\' : \'drill\'}</span><strong>{prior.title}</strong></Link> : <Link to={url(\'lessons\')}>All lessons</Link>}{next ? <Link to={url(next.id)}><span>Next {next.type === \'note\' ? \'lesson\' : \'drill\'}</span><strong>{next.title}<ArrowRight size={18}/></strong></Link> : <Link to={url(\'lessons\')}>Return to lessons<ArrowRight size={18}/></Link>}</nav>}\\r\\n    {!isIndex && view !== \'tools\' && !current && <div className=\\"oc-course-note\\"><h1>This lesson is not available here.</h1><Link to={url(\'lessons\')}>Return to lessons</Link></div>}\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 1.0 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"2a3ce8","wall_time_seconds":0.3269866,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1949,"output":"---\\r\\ntype: synthesis\\r\\nsubject: LSAT teaching voice standard\\r\\ncreated: 2026-10-02\\r\\nupdated: 2026-10-03\\r\\naliases: [LSAT voice reference, Conditional transcription writing standard]\\r\\ntags: [lsat-u, voice, pedagogy, writing]\\r\\nsources:\\r\\n  - ../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# LSAT teaching: make the reasoning sound like someone thinking\\r\\n\\r\\n**This is Joshua\'s selected reference for writing LSAT teaching material.** Use it for bootcamp lessons, lecture notes, explanations, guided examples, drills, flashcards, quizzes, reference pages, and instructional feedback. It develops the teaching-content register in [the canonical teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md). That document still governs correspondence and marketing in their own registers.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua selected the supplied **Conditional Reasoning** transcription on 2026-10-02 because of its writing, tone, word choice, cadence, point of view, progression, and depth. The goal is to reproduce those qualities closely through original wording and examples. The central quality is patient, conversational reasoning that the reader can follow and eventually perform.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is a calibration example. This guide separates **observed features** from **instructions for our material**. A source habit is not automatically a rule, a research finding, or permission to import a topic. Matching the voice does not require repeating the same metaphors, anecdotes, exercise sentences, or personal claims.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Find the part you need\\r\\n\\r\\n- [The evidence and coverage](#the-evidence-and-coverage)\\r\\n- [The voice in one original passage](#the-voice-in-one-original-passage)\\r\\n- [How the teacher relates to the reader](#how-the-teacher-relates-to-the-reader)\\r\\n- [Sentence length and spoken cadence](#sentence-length-and-spoken-cadence)\\r\\n- [Word choice and useful verbal habits](#word-choice-and-useful-verbal-habits)\\r\\n- [Questions that make the reader think](#questions-that-make-the-reader-think)\\r\\n- [Transitions, repetition, metaphor, and emphasis](#transitions-explain-why-the-next-move-follows)\\r\\n- [The complete source progression and depth](#the-complete-source-progression-and-depth)\\r\\n- [What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp](#what-to-carry-into-the-conditional-bootcamp)\\r\\n- [Accuracy and method boundaries](#accuracy-and-method-boundaries)\\r\\n- [Calibration examples and review](#calibration-examples-for-different-lsat-surfaces)\\r\\n- [A reusable writing brief](#a-reusable-writing-brief)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The evidence and coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [source summary](../wiki/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice.md) identifies the [preserved HTML](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/conditional_reasoning_transcription.html), [provenance](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/PROVENANCE.md), and SHA-256. Every supplied section, FAQ entry, table, worked diagram, and drill item was read. HTML line references below refer to that unchanged archived file.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe document has six main sections and six subordinate headings. It ends with six basic drill items and an answer-key reference. One line is explicitly marked partially obscured. The answer key is not supplied. This analysis covers the entire attachment; it cannot reconstruct the missing line or establish the contents of the larger chapter.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML says its formatting was adjusted. We can examine what a pause, table, side note, or separated example does for learning. We cannot claim its font, spacing, color, or CSS exactly reproduces the original publication. No author is identified in the file. The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. Clear teaching can be certain about the limits of what is known.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe teacher does not apologize for asking the reader to think. The explanation makes the request reasonable. In the FAQ, the narrator acknowledges early mistakes and explains the value of practicing anyway. The tone combines patience with a specific demand: attempt the question, write the diagram, inspect the error.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** state the consequence plainly and show why. Preserve legitimate uncertainty. Avoid changing a logical “could” into “must” to make the prose sound stronger. Avoid guarantees about learning outcomes, timing, or score changes unless we have evidence.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Warmth points at the work\\r\\n\\r\\nEncouragement is usually tied to an action. The reader can look back at the lesson, make a provisional attempt, learn from a wrong translation, or build confidence by checking work. The warmth comes from useful help and a teacher who expects progress.\\r\\n\\r\\nUseful form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> If the direction felt unclear, read the statement back in ordinary English. What does it say you need? Keep that complete idea in your diagram.\\r\\n\\r\\nWeak form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You\'ve got this! Conditionals are easy once you know the trick!\\r\\n\\r\\nThe weak version offers reassurance without a way forward and minimizes the actual difficulty.\\r\\n"}'}]

## assistant

**The main finding: the updated path you’re viewing is the opening section, not the entire Conditional Bootcamp.** It has nine notes and four drills. The broader curriculum contains 30 units, including advanced translation, chains, compound conditions, LR applications and quantifiers. Those later units haven’t been carried into the new course structure.

Here is the skeleton, with **drill instructions distinguished from the actual exercise**.

**First, understand what the rule tells you**

| Step | Note or drill | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Note: What conditionals are** | A conditional states a rule. It does not tell you that either condition actually occurred. Introduces what the rule guarantees, rather than what usually happens. Includes an inline check distinguishing the rule from a fact. |
| 2 | **Note: The sufficient condition** | What is enough to establish something else. Explains why sufficient does not mean the only possible way. Checks whether another route to the same result remains possible. |
| 3 | **Note: The necessary condition** | What the relationship requires. Explains why having the requirement does not guarantee the starting condition, and why “necessary” does not mean earlier in time. |
| 4 | **Drill: Enough, required, or still open?** | **Instructions page:** read the rule and supplied facts, decide what follows, check and revise. **Exercise:** seven tasks covering rules versus facts, applying a fact, sufficient and necessary roles, what remains open, and a case showing why reversal fails. |

These pieces establish the meaning before asking students to memorize indicator words or manipulate arrows.

**Then, translate the meaning accurately**

| Step | Note or drill | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | **Note: Read the must arrow** | Sufficient on the left, necessary on the right. The arrow expresses what must follow, without implying cause or chronological order. Builds a diagram incrementally and checks a sentence whose if-clause comes last. |
| 6 | **Note: Sufficient-condition words** | **If, when, where, all, the only, every and any.** Teaches what each expression refers to, retaining qualifications and reading the whole sentence. Includes wording variants, examples, checks and recall cards. |
| 7 | **Drill: Build the sufficient side** | **Instructions page:** identify the sufficient condition, build and read the diagram, then test the reverse. **Exercise:** target selection, diagram construction, the-only distinctions, equivalent wording and a constructed counterexample. |
| 8 | **Note: Necessary-condition words** | **Only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires and must.** Covers requirements appearing before or after the indicator. Also distinguishes permission or obligation from an action actually happening. |
| 9 | **Note: Keep the whole meaning** | Retain every qualification; identify the condition wherever it appears; distinguish **only** from **the only**; use a possible case to check whether the translation changes the rule. Includes embedded exercises. |
| 10 | **Drill: Conditional translation practice** | **Instructions page:** a short introduction and Start practice. **Inside the drill:** a separate briefing before each stage. The sequence is qualification checks → guided diagrams → independent writing and English readback → comparison of differently worded rules → unfamiliar cases. Mistakes lead to targeted fresh checks. |

This section moves from identifying the parts with help to making a translation before seeing supplied choices.

**Finally, reason backward without reversing the rule**

| Step | Note or drill | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | **Note: When a requirement is missing** | Derives the backward inference: if the required result is absent, the sufficient condition cannot hold. A four-case explorer distinguishes valid forward/backward reasoning from reversal and inverse errors. |
| 12 | **Note: Write and read the contrapositive** | Reverse the sides and negate both conditions. Handles existing negatives and the four sign patterns. Includes practical diagramming questions, a negative-case exercise and the one combination that violates a conditional. |
| 13 | **Drill: Put the whole process together** | **Instructions page:** identify both conditions, build the original and contrapositive, read them back, check and repair. **Exercise:** nine sentences covering indicator wording, qualifications, clause order and negative conditions on either or both sides. |

The opening order is verified in [the course path](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/openingCoursePath.ts:13). Its four separate drill instruction pages are defined in [the course screen](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/OpeningCourse.tsx:43).

**The broader bootcamp continues with these phases**

These topics are already authored in the recorded curriculum. They are not yet subsequent pages in the updated opening path.

| Phase | Notes and subject matter, in order |
|---|---|
| **Foundations** | Conditional meaning; sufficient versus necessary; sufficient indicators; necessary indicators; facts versus rules; whether a conclusion must follow; exact negation; reasoning backward from a missing requirement. Some of this overlaps the revised opening. |
| **Other translation forms** | **Group 3:** unless, until and without, including existing negatives and temporal boundaries. **Group 4:** conditions that cannot coexist. Then mixed translation across the four groups and guarantees without a familiar indicator. |
| **Connecting rules** | Link through the same condition. Recognize shared triggers, shared results and mismatched conditions that do **not** create a chain. Establish when a rule actually fires. |
| **More complex conditions** | AND versus OR; compound negation and De Morgan; population and time restrictions; biconditionals; negating the entire rule with a counterexample. |
| **Applying conditionals in LR** | Must Be True; sufficient assumption; necessary assumption; flaw; parallel reasoning; principle questions. Each teaches the operation needed for that question context. |
| **Quantifiers** | Meaning of some, most, all and no; exact negation; valid witness and majority links; unsupported overlap and invalid quantity chains. |

The later pattern is generally **note → guided example → skill drill → explanation and repair**. Unlike the four revised opening drills, later exercises generally put their directions on the exercise surface rather than on a separate Start page. The advanced material is authored in [the application curriculum](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/content/applications.source.ts:27).

**How this compares with Intro to LR Bootcamp**

The actual Intro to LR path is:

1. **Foundational notes:** the three parts of an LR question, arguments, premises, conclusions and conclusion types.
2. **Conclusion Type Lab:** isolate the first distinction.
3. **Further notes:** material beyond premises and conclusions, then the two-part conclusion check.
4. **Main Conclusion Lab:** combine those distinctions in fuller arguments.
5. **Structure note and lab:** first-sentence versus rebuttal structures, followed by a four-step exercise.
6. **Official-question practice:** transfer the method into LSAT questions.

Its useful pattern is:

**Teach the distinction → try it within the note → practise it in a focused drill → combine it with other skills → apply it in actual questions.**

Conditional’s opening now follows much of that pattern. Intro to LR carries the learner more clearly into question-level application and records attempts for later review. Its current sequence is verified in [the Intro to LR path](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/content/introToLrPath.ts:38).

**The curriculum holes I would address**

- **Connect the opening to the rest of the course.** Step 13 currently returns to Lessons. It should lead clearly into the next phase. This is the largest structural hole.
- **Give necessary-condition wording its own focused drill.** Sufficient wording gets one. Necessary wording moves into another note and then mixed practice. A short necessary-only drill would establish the skill before mixing both families.
- **Carry the instruction-page structure through the later phases.** Students should consistently understand what they are practising before starting.
- **Add cumulative practice across phases.** A learner who just studied “unless” should eventually have to distinguish it from only-if, ordinary if, compounds and chains without being told which procedure to use.
- **Make the bridge into LR questions explicit.** The later application notes exist, but they need a clear progression from isolated rules to arguments and question tasks.
- **Deepen review and retention checks.** Most later units have only three questions per difficulty band. Immediate correction shows useful practice; it does not establish lasting understanding. Written explanations also remain ungraded.

**My recommendation is to organize the complete course into six visible phases: meaning, translation, contraposition, linking and compound rules, LR application, then quantifiers.** Keep the opening’s note-and-drill rhythm throughout. The topic inventory is broad; the missing piece is a coherent path that connects it and tests whether students can use earlier skills as the work becomes harder.
